en: The Scripture on Mañjuśrī Manifesting the Treasure Store, Volume One, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery, together with...
He was accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty, and ten thousand bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Buddha sat in the Kāliṅga Lecture Hall, surrounded on all sides by an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands, as he preached the sūtra for them.

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, together with five hundred bodhisattvas, as well as the various devas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the retinues of the Four Heavenly Kings, all went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what Dharma did you teach just now?
We pray that the God among Gods will honor the discourse you have expounded."
The venerable Subhūti, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, addressed Mañjuśrī:
"Previously, the World-Honored One spoke concerning the disciples; may the Superior now speak concerning the conduct of bodhisattvas."
Mañjuśrī replied to Subhūti:
"The practices of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not the vessel for a bodhisattva; why then do you ask?"
He said, "I pray you will explain it; if I am truly a fit vessel, I shall listen and receive it.
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Venerable Subhūti!
How does one know who is a vessel?
And how is one not a vessel?"
Subhūti said: “Since all those disciples attain liberation through sound, how could we know who is a vessel and who is not?
We now ask you this; we wish most earnestly to hear your answer.”
Mañjuśrī replied: "Indeed, Subhūti!
Those who emerge from darkness are all not vessels for the Buddha-dharma."

Even if one provides illumination for those in darkness, one does not fall into darkness; by rescuing and protecting sentient beings, one does not conjoin with darkness, but becomes a vessel for the Buddha-dharma for all that exists.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If one studies with limitations and, having completed that study of the Dharma, looks upon all people and sees those who take what is not given, feels fear in their mind, loathes them with revulsion, and fears the three realms without finding joy in them, then such a person is not a vessel for the teachings of the Buddhas."

If one governs the future for many thousands of kalpas yet has not yet set out, wandering through the three realms without fear, remaining free from the three defilements and taking delight in birth and death as if strolling through gardens, pavilions, and pleasure groves, gladdening all beings, and whose coming and going are devoid of the six matters—this is called being a vessel for the Buddha-dharma.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

A bodhisattva manifests the presence of desire yet has no delight in desire; manifests anger yet has no malice or harm; manifests delusion yet has no darkness; and manifests wickedness, stubbornness, and cruelty as a butcher yet is free from defilement."

Now, acting as the true guide for those in the three realms who have no leader, remaining harmonious and not wild amidst the turmoil, practicing humility and courtesy toward those who are arrogant, removing the heavy burdens of all sentient beings, instructing everyone so that the Three Jewels are never interrupted, and attaining the three types of supernormal knowledge to manifest everywhere—this is what is called being a vessel for the Buddhadharma.
Thereupon, Subhūti asked Mañjuśrī: "All dharmas are equal;
they all equally share the same single primordial limit (*koṭi*).
How can one know who is a vessel and who is not?"
Mañjuśrī replied:

"For example, Subhūti, it is like a potter who takes clay of a single uniform quality and fashions various vessels from it. All are placed together in one location and fired; some may hold clarified butter (*ghṛta*), some sesame oil, some nectar or honey, and some impurities. Yet the clay itself remains of one kind, without any differentiation.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

All dharmas are equal and fundamentally one; their ultimate limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is one. Yet, when they arise through conditions and proceed into activity, distinctions emerge. In this regard, the vessels for clarified butter and oil represent disciples and *pratyekabuddhas*; the vessel for ambrosial honey represents all *bodhisattvas*; and the impure vessel represents those who are like lowly, ordinary worldlings.
He asked Mañjuśrī again:
"Can those who are vessels be made into non-vessels?
He replied:
"He may simply be unfit as a vessel.
Subhūti asked: "By what causes and conditions?"
He replied: "Yes, Subhūti!
Those who possess the vessels for receiving all sensual desires abide within existence; furthermore, those who are able to sever all sensual desires are none of them vessels for the Buddha-dharma."
He asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! What high or low distinctions are there among vessels?"
He replied: "Indeed, Subhūti!
A vessel has neither height nor depth."
He asked again:
"How is this so, Mañjuśrī?"
"Are there no distinctions of high or low among vessels? He replied:
"In truth, there is neither high nor low; because that which the Dharma abides in has no high or low, it constitutes a vessel that is firm and solid."
If there were such things as superior or inferior courses of action, one would know that this is a vessel of destruction.
Indeed, Subhūti!
It is like space, which is not a vessel for all medicinal herbs, trees, plants, and myriad things.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva is a vessel for all Buddha-dharmas, and there is no other vessel [greater than this].
It is like a tree growing from the earth: the void is able to receive it and cause it to grow into a great vessel.
"In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva gives rise to pure and equanimous intentions, and by relying on the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they attain growth and development.
He asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! How does a bodhisattva achieve growth and development?
He replied:
"Just as that which is nurtured by space is likewise the bodhisattva;
both space and the bodhisattva ultimately neither increase nor diminish."
He asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! What does this statement mean?"
He replied,
"It neither increases defilements nor diminishes the Buddha-dharma.
He asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! What difference is there between dust and the Buddha-dharma?
He replied:

"Just as those near Mount Sumeru are illuminated by its radiance so that they all appear with a single aspect, becoming golden in color, so it is with the Bodhisattva: through the light of wisdom, he eliminates all defilements, causing them to share his own appearance, which is the color of the Buddha-dharma."
"Indeed, Subhūti!
For this reason, all sensory objects are the Buddha-dharma. Those of clear wisdom should contemplate them as being equal and without distinction; all dharmas are called the Buddha-dharma."
He asked again:
"Why do you say that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma?
He replied:
"What you have done is as that which all Buddhas have performed.
He asked again:
"How is it so, Mañjuśrī?"
"What is it like that which the Buddha has done?
He replied, "It is like the fundamental and the derivative being likewise; that which is such as neither increasing nor decreasing is called 'suchness' (tathatā)."
He asked again:
"Mañjuśrī, what is meant by 'the root'?"
"What is meant by 'the root and the branch'? He replied:
"The root is emptiness and the branch is stillness; this is what is called the root and the branch."
He asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! What is the difference between emptiness and quiescence?"
He replied,
“For example, is there any difference between gold and a jewel? Subhūti said:
"The substance is of one kind; it is merely that the names differ.
He replied, "It is so.
Emptiness and stillness are merely different names; the wise do not become attached to words and numbers."
He asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! What is called the characteristic of delusion?"
"What is the characteristic of wisdom? He replied:
"As taught by the Buddha, conditioned origination is the characteristic of delusion; the meaning of the Dharma is the characteristic of wisdom."
He asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! What constitutes the characteristic of causal conditions?"
He replied: "Subhūti,
it is the characteristic of the twelve links of dependent origination."
This is the characteristic of causal conditions:
if there is mental formation, there is then perception and cognition; if there were no mental formation and no perception, then cognition would not manifest.
That deluded person gives rise to mental formations, and thus these come to have verbal expression and cognition.
The wise person does not create through conceptualization, and thus there is no verbal expression or cognition;

if they abide nowhere, they then reach universal pervasiveness. This is the practice of the noble ones among practices that have practice; that which is without practice is not the practice of the noble ones.
Subhūti asked again:
"Mañjuśrī, what is meant by 'noble and holy ones'?"
He replied,
"The noble and holy ones are those who travel through space leaving no trace.
He asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! Are all dharmas, moreover, governed by the stainless emptiness and so forth?
He replied:
"So it is. Subhūti asked again:
"By what cause is this so?"
Mañjuśrī said: “For example, just as all waters flow into the great ocean and merge to become a single taste;
so it is, Subhūti!”
"By means of the stainless emptiness and so forth, one governs all phenomena, making them all of a single flavor, in order to liberate sentient beings.
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is it that is called liberation? He replied:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
"For what reason is there obstruction?
He replied,
"It is because of the absence of wisdom that there is obstruction."
He replied:
“So it is, Subhūti! It is because of liberating those who lack wisdom that one speaks of liberation.”
He asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! Since all dharmas are without distinction, from where does this discourse on the existence of wisdom and the absence of wisdom arise?"
He replied:
"For example, Subhūti, it is like speaking of water during the heat of the summer months, and likewise speaking of water during the cold of winter; the water itself does not differ.
In the same way, Subhūti..."

Because their perceptions are not pure, they possess defilement; because they possess defilement, there is the teaching of "lack of wisdom. Those who cultivate pure perceptions are free from attachment; therefore, regarding those true persons, there is the teaching of "wisdom," yet there is no intermediate teaching of being either wise or unwise.
Subhūti asked again:
"Mañjuśrī, does that meaning travel far?"
He replied:
"Because there are two types of practice. Subhūti said:
"Mañjuśrī, is the meaning difficult to see?
He replied:
"It is for the sake of being separated from the eye of wisdom. Subhūti said:
"Is its meaning difficult to uphold?"
Mañjuśrī replied, “It cannot be grasped. Subhūti said:
"Why is its meaning difficult to understand?
He replied, "Because it is not understood."
Subhūti said, "Is the meaning difficult to comprehend?
He replied:
"Because one has already become detached from all discursive thoughts. Subhūti said:
"Is its meaning difficult to explain?"
He replied,
"Because they are empty and so forth. Subhūti said:
"Is 'principle' (artha) the absence of thought?
He replied, "It functions through the practice of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñā)."
Subhūti asked, "Is 'meaning' (artha) non-conceptualization?
He replied:
"Therefore, there is no verbal expression. Subhūti asked:
"Does this mean that there are no noble sages?"
He replied, "Therefore,
one is free from conceptualization and aspiration. Subhūti said:
"What is the meaning of 'the wise manifesting knowledge'?
He replied, "It is for this reason that they do not see themselves."
Subhūti asked again:
"Mañjuśrī, if the Tathāgata were to say:..."
"One who seeks the meaning of profit does not obtain that meaning, while one who does not seek the meaning of profit obtains it.
For whom was this passage spoken? Mañjuśrī replied:
"Indeed, Subhūti! That which is the benefit of meaning (artha) is non-attainment.
If one were to seek or desire to attain that meaning, there would be no benefit in that meaning; for that meaning is the meaning of quiescence (śānta)."

If that person, with thoughts directed toward the body, seeks to obtain benefit and profit, this constitutes failing to obtain benefit and profit regarding what is truly meaningful. As the Buddha said:
"One who does not seek meaning obtains meaning; one who seeks meaning, on the contrary, does not obtain it."
Subhūti asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! Why does the Buddha say that all dharmas are entirely non-dharmas?”
Mañjuśrī replied: "Indeed, Subhūti!
As the World-Honored One has said in the Parable Sūtra:"
"One should eliminate even those dharmas that are desired, let alone those that are contrary to the Dharma!
If they are eliminated, such dharmas are precisely what is called 'not being contrary to the Dharma.'"
Subhūti asked again: “How is this, Mañjuśrī?
Is the Buddha-dharma not, in fact, non-dharma?”
He replied: "No.
The Buddha-dharma has no flourishing; that which does not flourish is what is called the Dharma."
As the Buddha has said:
"All dharmas are non-dharmas. Subhūti said:
"It is unprecedented and most difficult to equal!
Mañjuśrī, that a newly initiated bodhisattva, upon hearing this teaching, would not be terrified— this is truly marvelous."
Mañjuśrī said: "Indeed, Subhūti!
There are four things by which the offspring of a lion, upon hearing the lion’s roar, does not feel fear or dread, nor do their hairs stand on end."
What are the four?
First, his lineage is authentic;
second, he is born of a lioness.
Third, being nurtured by the Venerable One;
fourth, not clinging to any state of existence.
These are the four.

A practitioner such as this is a true seed of the Tathāgata and a bodhisattva of sincere truth; born from the Tathāgata and advanced by the Dharma, they transcend the level of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and thus do not belong to their class.

Upon hearing the teaching that all phenomena are thus, he will never feel fear; in whatever he preaches or says, he will be without dread or trepidation, his hair will not stand on end, and his mind will be neither indolent nor hesitant or timid.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When a fledgling bird soars through the void of space, does it have any fear?
He replied:
"No," said Mañjuśrī. "It is so, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva dwells in the realm of emptiness, they hear all dharmas without fear; regarding all phenomena, they are neither apprehensive nor hesitant, nor do they encounter any doubt or difficulty. Because they have thoroughly understood all dharmas, when they hear whatever is taught, they are neither afraid nor apprehensive, remaining free from dread.
Mañjuśrī said to Subhūti,
"From what does fear arise?
He replied:
"Because one uses craving to view the body, there is fear.
Mañjuśrī said: "A bodhisattva, by knowing the body through craving, is not afraid of what is taught regarding all phenomena, nor does he experience any terror."
Subhūti asked: “Mañjuśrī!
If a bodhisattva realizes tranquility and does not crave the body, how can they attain the Way?”
Mañjuśrī replied, “Indeed, Subhūti!

A bodhisattva does not perceive the attainment of the Way as being characterized by attachment to the body. If a bodhisattva were to perceive the attainment of the Way as being characterized by attachment to the body, for that reason they would not attain the Way.”
Subhūti said: "Yes, Mañjuśrī!
A bodhisattva practices through the employment of great skillful means; does a bodhisattva not see that attachment to the body prevents the attainment of the Way?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Indeed, Subhūti!

A bodhisattva, having received the skillful means of wisdom, possesses this noble nature of a bodhisattva; for this reason, the bodhisattva knows that by clinging to the body, one does not attain the Way."

It is like taking a sharp axe to cut down a great tree, sectioning it piece by piece and then reassembling them back in their original positions; it returns to its former state and never falls to the ground. In this way, the Bodhisattva possesses wisdom and skillful means as his noble nature; therefore, the Bodhisattva knows that attachment to the body does not lead to the Way.
Just as when it rains heavily and trees grow lushly, producing stems, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits that benefit all;

so too does the Bodhisattva, practicing great compassion and kindness, knowing those who are attached to their bodies, manifest in various forms within the three realms and benefit sentient beings according to their respective appearances.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Should a torrential rain or a violent wind arise to blow down that tree, the Bodhisattva, by means of great wisdom, releases a gentle, great rain, which then falls again beneath the Buddha-tree.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”

Please speak quickly of how the wisdom and skillful means of the bodhisattvas constitute their noble nature, and explain how they thus practice the dharma of great loving-kindness and great compassion. Now, Mañjuśrī!
Furthermore, listen again to what I say.

Suppose there is a country that is both powerful and vast; clouds and mists arise on all sides, and great hot stones are cast down, intending to incinerate that land so that all its grasses and trees would be burned. Yet, it then rains down floods with drops as thick as axle-trees, causing all the grasses and trees to grow everywhere.
It is thus, Mañjuśrī!

The Bodhisattva rains down wisdom and skillful means, manifesting through expedient means as entering among all ignorant and ordinary people; he instructs those in darkness by manifesting the conduct of sages and worthies, and for those who observe the precepts within birth and death, he reveals the meaning to bring them joy.

"It is like a fragrant tree, whose roots are fragrant, its trunk fragrant, its branches fragrant, its leaves fragrant, its flowers fragrant, and its fruits fragrant, each being distinct from the others;

likewise, by means of the natural nature of wisdom-activities, a bodhisattva accords with the desires of all people and preaches the Dharma according to their fundamental conduct, causing each to rejoice and their minds to be opened and liberated, without ever abandoning the foundation of great compassion."

"It is like the great mani jewel named Śakrābhilagnaka; when Śakra, Lord of Devas, wears this jewel, it illuminates his garments, his court ladies, his houses, his lecture halls, and his palaces, such that everything appears as pure radiance, yet the great moon-like mani jewel has no thought.
In the same way, the fruit of a bodhisattva’s clear wisdom is like the moon-like mani jewel—purely liberated and universally manifesting all meanings, forever free from conceptualization."
The Buddha said, “Mañjuśrī!

It is like a great moon-precious gem named ‘Bestower of All Wishes,’ which, according to the desires of beings, causes them all to be fully satisfied and obtain abundance; yet even while bestowing these wish-granting jewels, it has no thought.”
In this way, the Bodhisattva is pure like a jewel, fulfilling all the desires and aspirations of sentient beings, yet that Bodhisattva remains free from conceptualization.
"Just as when a great fire breaks out in the midst of space and a heavy rain falls, the space itself is neither cold nor hot;
likewise, while the Bodhisattva dwells amidst the fires of the triple world, if they abide in the realm of quiescent non-action (*asaṃskṛta*), they experience neither cold nor heat."

"Just as in the midst of empty space, poisonous trees may grow and medicinal trees may also grow; yet that poisonous tree does not harm the empty space, nor does the fragrance of the medicinal tree require anything to be removed or purified.

In this same way, the Bodhisattva, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), enters among all poisonous trees so that they may attain fulfillment. Using the trunk and nodes of the medicinal tree to protect the roots, the various defilements and afflictions do not adhere to the Bodhisattva. While purifying the faculties, there is nothing to be purified; he enters both matters simultaneously without being stained by either."
"It is like a leaking vessel: if one merely patches a single spot so that it no longer leaks, yet leaves the rest unpatched so that they all continue to leak;

likewise, a Bodhisattva who dwells in constant concentration and possesses great supernormal powers has no other leakage, yet wherever he dwells, he manifests various forms of leakage, manifesting births and preaching the Dharma in accordance with the fundamental dispositions of all beings."
"Just as a fine steed of dappled hue, possessing great strength and power, protects its fellow horses and does not greedily guard itself;
so too the Bodhisattva, established in great compassion with great strength and power, transcends all other powers to rescue and protect all people, without thinking of his own person."
"Just as a fierce lion, the king of beasts, has nothing to fear except for a great fire;
so too, the Bodhisattva has no fears, save for the fear of falling into the stages of the Śrāvaka or the Pratyekabuddha."
"Just as the dragon king Elāpattra, though he is a beast, is able to manifest pure transformations— all of which result from the fundamental virtues of Śakra—
so too does a bodhisattva, even if fallen among the beasts, is able to manifest and preach all pure dharmas, guiding them according to their own past conduct."
"Just as fire is produced by drilling wood and light is emitted by a bright jewel— wherein both provide benefit— so it is, Mañjuśrī!

Whether there be a bodhisattva who has first resolved for enlightenment or one who will resolve for enlightenment after sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, these two types of bodhisattvas alike eliminate all the dust of defilement and burn away all arduous sufferings."

"Just as various trees each have their own names, differing in color, distinct in branches and leaves, and dissimilar in flowers and fruits—yet all these trees flourish by means of the four great elements;

so too, a bodhisattva who practices various conducts and accumulates many roots of virtue does so entirely for the sake of the aspiration for enlightenment, and by universally encouraging and assisting toward omniscience, achieves fulfillment."
"Just as wherever a Wheel-Turning Sage King goes, the seven treasures and the fourfold army all follow him;

so too, when a Bodhisattva attains the perfection of wisdom through skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), there is nowhere he does not enter, and all the dharmas of the various paths and categories follow him."
"Just as, for example, the king of the kalaviṅka birds, even if he falls into a net, continues to utter his plaintive song; so it is, Mañjuśrī!"

Even if a bodhisattva should fall into a nest-like den, failing to realize the Buddha-dharma, not destroying attachment to the body, and not emerging from the triple world, they continue to let out the lion’s roar of awakening, preaching the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and expounding upon the matter of non-origination and non-extinction.
"Just as the king of the kalaviṅka birds dwells upon a mountain peak and refuses to sing until he finds his own kind, whereupon he utters his melodious cry; even so, Mañjuśrī!"

If there is a bodhisattva who enters among the disciples, he does not discourse on the inconceivable Buddha-voice; rather, when among other bodhisattvas, he speaks of the matters of bodhisattvas and discourses on the inconceivable voice of the Buddha.
"Just as the wind of the Svarabhañjana cannot sustain the earth, nor the firm Jambudvīpa, its trees, lecture halls, or dwellings;
so it is, Mañjuśrī!"

All disciples and pratyekabuddhas are unable to endure the inconceivable names of the Buddha-dharma, nor the pure transformations of the Buddha’s supernormal powers; even those who possess faith and are free from doubt do not achieve this through their own merit alone.
It is all through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power that they are enabled to attain faith.
"For example, when the light of the sun shines upon both the pure and the impure, it feels neither joy nor aversion; the celestial palaces of the sun and moon never suffer eclipse.

In the same way, the Bodhisattva emits the light of wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*), engaging in various activities alongside disciples, *pratyekabuddhas*, and ordinary worldlings. He does not feel delight because he is among the disciples, nor does he feel sorrow or distress because he is among ordinary worldlings, yet he never loses the sphere of his bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom."
“Suppose, for example, when the leaves first begin to sprout on the Pārijāta tree in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, all the devas see it and are filled with joy, thinking to themselves:
‘The Pārijāta tree will soon have flowers and fruit, and its fruition will be realized.’”
"In this way, Mañjuśrī!

If a bodhisattva gives away all that they possess without begrudging anything, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, will praise that bodhisattva, saying: 'Before long, this one shall attain the flowers and gifts of the Buddha-dharma and bestow them upon all living beings.'"
"Just as a tree that is supple yet has deep and firm roots will not fear falling, even if its branches appear bent;
so it is, Mañjuśrī! If there is a bodhisattva who reverently honors and serves all people, they will never fear falling into the stages of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha."
"Just as water falls upon the earth and flows away;
so too does the Bodhisattva, being free from pride, prostrate and take refuge in omniscience.
Just as the great ocean, established upon the earth, is the first to be formed and receives all the currents of rivers and streams;"
In this way, because the Bodhisattva is free from pride, he attains the pinnacle of all Buddha-dharmas.

"For example, there is a great moon-precious gem named 'Illuminator,' from which all that is desired emerges; no other moon-precious gems can equal it, for it illuminates all other moon-precious gems without its own radiance ever diminishing.
Likewise, the Bodhisattva instructs his disciples and pratyekabuddhas, causing them to enter the discipline and not fall into those [limited] practices."
"Just as the māndārava flower is soft, exquisite, and its fragrance is perceived for forty li in every direction;
so it is with the Bodhisattva, who, through the wisdom of the noble ones, gives rise to great compassion and brings peace and security to all sentient beings everywhere."
"Just as when there is a sick person who smells the fragrance of the māndārava flower, their illness is immediately cured;

so it is with the Bodhisattva, who, through the practice of the fragrance of great loving-kindness and great compassion, reaches everywhere to eliminate and resolve the illnesses of all worldly afflictions."
"For example, when there is no Buddha, the udumbara tree produces fruit without flowers;
likewise, as long as there is no Bodhisattva, the flowers of the Buddha-dharma do not emerge.
It is like the Dragon King Anavatapta: whenever he sends down rain, it falls everywhere throughout Jambudvīpa."
In this way, when the Bodhisattva releases the rain of Dharma, it pervades all people and even the crawling insects.
Just as the four great rivers flow from the great abyss of Lake Anavatapta and all return to the ocean, which is thereby constantly filled;
so too does the Bodhisattva flow with the practice of the four debts of gratitude, thereby fully completing the great ocean of wisdom.
“Mañjuśrī, it is like this: before there was a great ocean, the people of Jambudvīpa obtained small, naturally occurring maṇi jewels;
in the same way, Mañjuśrī, before one has resolved to attain the mind of a bodhisattva, all rely upon and employ the Dharma-jewels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
"Just as whatever possesses form and appearance is composed of the four great elements, so it is with the Bodhisattva:
all the teachings they proclaim are intended to deliver all beings and cause them to enter the gateway of the Dharma."
"Just as trees growing amidst mountains and marshes are of no benefit to the multitude;
so it is with disciples who, fearing the perils of birth and death, are of no benefit to all beings."
Just as a medicinal tree growing in the center of a great city provides healing for many people, so too does the Bodhisattva enter into great compassion and give rise to omniscience;
with a jewel-like mind, they bring vast benefit to all living beings.
"Just as rainwater from the heavens cannot remain for long;
so it is with a disciple, who does not endure long after being instructed and taught the Dharma.
Just as in the spring months, great flowing rivers never reach exhaustion;"
In this way, the Bodhisattva teaches and expounds the Dharma so that it may endure for a long time.
"It is like the trees growing on a mountain in winter: if they are cut down, they grow back quickly in due season; even so, Mañjuśrī!"
"Regarding that which the Buddha manifests: although the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, the teaching of the Three Jewels shall not be severed.
Thereupon, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is unprecedented, World-Honored One!"
The names, virtues, and practices of these bodhisattvas are so lofty and immeasurable that none can fully extol them.
Furthermore, the true and authentic merits that the Tathāgata has just now expounded are likewise difficult to equal.
"If a bodhisattva, upon hearing such virtues and meanings, feels neither joy nor sorrow, this is most excellent!
The Buddha said, "This is brought about by the fundamental purity of the bodhisattva; therefore, when hearing it said that all such virtues and meanings are not good, they do not grieve."
Subhūti asked the Buddha,
"What is meant by 'primordial purity'?
The World-Honored One replied:

"The root of non-self, the root of no life-span, the root of no attachment to the body, and the root of no delusion or affection—these are the roots of 'mine' and 'not mine. In this way, the bodhisattva practices purity regarding these various roots."
Subhūti asked again:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘purity’?”
The Buddha said:
"Neither grasping nor abandoning is called purity;
neither arising nor ceasing is called purity."
To be without thought, without perception, without defilement, and without purity—this is called purity.
To be without high and without low—this is called purity.
To neither act nor not act, to be neither dark nor bright, to be without dust and without strife, and to be neither liberated nor bound—this is called purity.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If there is neither birth-and-death nor nirvāṇa, what is it that is called ‘purity’?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Such is purity: not dwelling on nirvana and not distancing oneself from birth-and-death; only then is one pure.
Just as space is pure, yet there is no one who purifies space, so too is the practitioner pure;
there is no agent who makes that [purity] pure. If, upon hearing this, one does not feel fear, this is called purity."
The Buddha said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Is there any dharma that is pure?"
Subhūti said to the Buddha,
“It has been pure from the very beginning.
The Buddha said:
"One who hears what is taught does not cling to the words; this is called purity. But as for one who clings to that which is non-investigative, can they be said to be pure?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The dharma-realm is naturally pure, yet there is equal knowledge of it."
The Buddha said:
"How is this so, Subhūti?"
"Can the dharma-realm be known?
Subhūti replied,
"It can be known."
The Buddha said:

"If the Dharma were to have cognition and thus arise, it would immediately become a different dharma. One seeks the Dharma-realm for that reason, yet that Dharma-realm itself does not cognize the Dharma."

The Buddha said, “Suppose, Subhūti, that there were no knowledge of liberation within the remaining dharma-realm; one who knows the dharma-realm would not attain liberation. In this way, how could one fully comprehend the dharma-realm?”
At that time, the venerable Subhūti remained silent and did not answer;
thereupon, Mañjuśrī addressed Subhūti:
"How is it, venerable one?"
“Does the World-Honored One have a teaching that he remains silent and does not answer? Subhūti replied,
“The reason for his silence is that they fundamentally did not give rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment.”
"Why is this? The eloquence of disciples is limited and obstructed, whereas the eloquence of bodhisattvas is limitless and unobstructed.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"Subhūti, what do you think?
Does the dharma-realm have any limitation or obstruction?
He replied:
"The Dharma-realm is infinite and unimpeded.
Mañjuśrī said, "If the Dharma-realm is indeed infinite and unimpeded, why, O worthy one, do you speak of silence as being obstructed?"
Subhūti replied:
“Those who wish to know the dharma-realm as something that can be exhausted will find verbal expression to be an obstruction;
however, those who understand that the dharma-realm is immeasurable and inexhaustible will not be hindered when hearing what is said.”
He asked again:
"What do you think, Subhūti?
As for the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), does it have an end?"
He replied, “It cannot be exhausted;
because the Dharma is the universal gate, for this reason the Dharma cannot be exhausted. Mañjuśrī said:
"If the Dharma is indeed inexhaustible, why is it that when the worthy one preaches the Dharma, there is obstruction?
He replied:

"It is because my disciples have limits that what they preach and expound has exhaustion and obstruction; yet when observing the Buddha-realm, it is immeasurable, and in preaching the Dharma-realm, there is no time of exhaustion."
Mañjuśrī asked again: "How so, Subhūti?"
"Can the Dharma further have a realm that can be described?
If one treats the Dharma as a realm, then the teaching of the Dharma would possess divisions.
He replied:
"I do not say that dharmas have a sphere of activity, nor that dharmas lack a sphere of activity.
Mañjuśrī said: "Why is this so, worthy one?"
"Does he speak of various realms?
Subhūti replied:
"As previously stated, the eloquence of the disciples is limited and obstructed, whereas the eloquence of a bodhisattva is limitless and unobstructed."
Mañjuśrī said: "How is it, worthy one!
Do you possess clear wisdom?"
Subhūti replied,
"In this way, one attains clear wisdom.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
“Worthy one, why do you say that silence constitutes an obstruction? He replied:
“Because my disciples are unable to fully comprehend the faculties of all people, I employ verbal expression, which serves as an obstruction.”
"The Bodhisattva’s eloquence and wisdom clearly understand the fundamental nature of sentient beings; therefore, he does not allow verbal expression to become an obstacle. Mañjuśrī said:
"World-Honored One, the wisdom of eloquence has no coming or going; could there possibly be any limitation to that conceptualization of wisdom?"
He replied: "No!
That which possesses wisdom has no characteristic of obstruction and no characteristic of abiding."
Mañjuśrī said: "If wisdom has the characteristic of being unimpeded and the characteristic of having no abode, for what reason, O worthy one, do you remain silent and create an obstruction?"
Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, the Buddha has praised your wisdom as supreme; you should question this worthy one, who will explain it for you."
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"Do you wish to hear me speak of the Dharma taught by Mañjuśrī?
I shall now proclaim it."
Why is this? I have heard that in the past, Mañjuśrī expounded the Dharma before countless hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, causing all the great disciples to remain silent and speechless.

Furthermore, I recall that in the past, Mañjuśrī and I traveled together eastward to visit various Buddha-fields, crossing through countless hundreds of thousands of buddha-lands. There was a world named *Priyaprasāda-viśuddha*, where the Buddha was named Prabhāśrī Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides there, preaching the Dharma.
He had a great disciple named Āryajñānapradīpa, whose wisdom was most supreme.

Seeing that the Tathāgata was dwelling in quiet seclusion and sitting in meditation, the disciple Āryajñānapradīpa immediately leaped up and ascended to the seventh Brahma-heaven. There, his voice resounded throughout the trichiliocosm, preaching the Dharma for the sake of all beings.

I, together with Mañjuśrī, arrived in that land, accompanied by countless hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas and one hundred thousand devas; we all followed as attendants to Mañjuśrī, desiring to hear the Dharma.

At that time, Mañjuśrī went to the Ābhāsvara Heaven and let out a great coughing sound; its resonance pervaded the trichiliocosm, shaking the palaces of Māra, extinguishing all evil realms, and causing beings to attain joy and faith.

Thereupon, the great disciple of the Lamp of Holy Wisdom, hearing that majestic sound, was immediately seized with great terror; he instantly collapsed to the ground, unable to control himself, just as when the great Sūlana wind arises, all things are blown down and none can maintain their stability.

At that time, the Holy Wisdom-Lamp was struck with awe; his hair stood on end as he experienced something unprecedented, and he went to the presence of the Tathāgata Prabhāśrī and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"O Heaven among Heavens!..."
"Who is this who, in the form of a bhikṣu, has uttered such a great sound?
Hearing his voice, I was so terrified that I could not control myself and immediately fell to the ground, like the trees that cannot avoid being crushed and blown down by the rising Sūlana wind."
That Buddha replied:

"There is a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī who has attained the stage of non-retrogression. By the power of his supernormal faculties, noble bliss, and clear wisdom, he has come to this land desiring to see the Tathāgata, prostrate in salutation, and inquire about various meanings."

Previously, you manifested your form in the Ābhāsvara Heaven and raised a great, resonant voice that was heard throughout the trichiliocosm; it shook the palaces of Māra, extinguished the evil realms, and caused all beings to rejoice.
The disciple addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to see Mañjuśrī.
O, Heaven among Heavens!"
"It would be a most great fortune to behold such as these noble beings.
At that moment, the Buddha Prabhāśrī manifested a spiritual resonance and invited Mañjuśrī.

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, together with the various bodhisattvas and devas, suddenly descended from the void and proceeded to the place where the Tathāgata Prabhāśrī was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and each, by means of their supernormal powers, manifested a Dharma-seat upon which they sat.
At that time, the Buddha Prabhāśrī asked Mañjuśrī:
“Virtuous one, for what reason have you come to this world?
What do you intend to observe and gather?”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
“I have come here wishing to see the World-Honored One, to prostrate and pay my respects, and to inquire about matters concerning the Dharma.
He asked again:
“Mañjuśrī! How does one contemplate the Tathāgata so as to achieve pure vision?
How does one pay homage to the Tathāgata?”
How does one inquire after the Tathāgata’s well-being?
How does one engage in discussion and questioning?
How does one listen to and receive what the Tathāgata has taught?
Mañjuśrī said: “To contemplate the quiescence of all phenomena is to see the Tathāgata as pure.

This pure contemplation is also without body, without thought, and without mind; it is without ritual, without reverence, without haste, and without violence; it is without destruction and without abiding; it is not permanently obtainable, born from emptiness, devoid of mental activity, and eternally serene—to contemplate in this way is to contemplate the Tathāgata.”
Yet there is no self; one does not treat form as equal, nor regard equality as equal, nor regard the heterodox as heterodox, for all is one in equality.

The Dharma-body of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is one's own body. One sees that which enters the Dharma-body, yet there is neither seeing nor anything seen; there is neither distance nor proximity. To act in this way is to pay homage to the Tathāgata.

He poses a question of profound stillness, without conceptualization, without perceiving any phenomena, and without even perceiving the phenomenon of "stillness. Having already attained stillness himself, he remains silent regarding all phenomena; he asks with equanimity and without confusion.

Whether there be one who desires to ask or one who asks, there is no duality therein; seeking the *pāramitā* of deliverance, they purify the three sites of enlightenment through their inquiry—this is how one pays homage to the Tathāgata.

Just as there is no going when one asks about non-going, and no sinking or floating, so too his words were gentle and compliant, in accord with the Tathāgata’s intent; he delighted the entire assembly without clinging to the minds of others. By means of these questions, he established countless people in the principles of the Path, never casting off the armor of virtue until they sat beneath the Bodhi tree. To listen to such a discourse and to question the Tathāgata in this manner is true inquiry.
Then the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One Prabhāśrī praised the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
It is as you have said, O worthy one; it is fitting that you behold the Tathāgata, prostrate yourself in salutation, and inquire about the meaning of the Dharma."
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī asked the great disciple Prabhāketu:
"Venerable One, how do you perceive the Tathāgata when prostrating in salutation?"
"What is the inquiry into the meaning of the Dharma? He replied: "Yes, Mañjuśrī!"
"I am not equal to this, nor am I of its kind; my disciples attain liberation through sound, yet they do not understand this matter.
He asked again:
"Venerable sir, when you realize it with the mind, do you say that liberation is attained through the realization of faith?"
He replied: "Mañjuśrī!
I have spoken only in a general way; I have not yet expounded the profound meaning."
Again he asked:
"What is meant by the equality of expounding and elucidating the profound meaning?
He replied:
"It does not govern impartiality, nor does it guide toward profound meaning.
It further says:
"How can one speak of the arising and ceasing of emptiness as being without profundity, yet attain the meaning of emptiness without the notion of impartiality?"
"Thus, this constitutes one form of thorough examination, which is the profound entry into the meaning of sincerity and truth.
[The interlocutor] asked:
"When newly initiated bodhisattvas hear these words, will they not fall into fear?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "Virtuous one, you are already afraid now; how much more so would those who have newly begun their studies be?
The Noble Wisdom said:
"I am one whom no one can frighten.
He replied,
"Why were you frightened just now?"
"Does the worthy one attain liberation through lack of weariness?
He replied,
"It is not by being without fear, nor by being without weariness, that one attains liberation."
Mañjuśrī said: "Virtuous one, because you were originally joined with fear, it is said that you, O benevolent one, are already afraid; how much more so for those who are newly trained!"
He asked Mañjuśrī,
“By what cause does a bodhisattva attain liberation?
He replied:
"Attaining fearlessness and being free from revulsion.
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"What does this mean? He replied:

"It means not fearing hundreds of thousands of millions of Māras and their retinues; preaching the Dharma for the sake of all beings without weariness; not fearing the accumulation of merit and the amassing of immeasurable virtues; and planting countless seeds of wisdom while never tiring in one's practice."
At that time, there were various devas in the assembly, each holding diverse and extraordinary flowers, which they scattered over Mañjuśrī. They all spoke together, saying:

"The place where Mañjuśrī dwells should be viewed with equanimity; this is the true majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata. Wherever Mañjuśrī is present, he provides protection and preaches the Dharma for the sake of saving and delivering all people through every virtue."
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī addressed the disciple Pradīpadhvaja:
"The World-Honored One has praised the wisdom of the elders; in what sense is this wisdom conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?"
"If the conditioned were to exist, it would be subject to arising; even if the unconditioned were to exist, it too would possess the characteristic of being produced.
Mañjuśrī replied: "That which all the noble sages contemplate is exclusively the discourse on the unconditioned."
He asked again:
"Does the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) possess thought or speech?
He replied:
"No. Mañjuśrī asked again: "For what purpose do the various sages and worthies preach the practice of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?"
At that time, the disciple Jñānapradīpa remained silent and offered no reply.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Prabhāśrī addressed Mañjuśrī:

"Preach this Dharma-gate for the sake of this assembly, so that the devas may hear and receive its teaching, and so that the bodhisattvas who hear it shall establish themselves in non-retrogression and attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path."
Mañjuśrī said: "That which is the gateway of the True Dharma practices in stillness; within the gate of stillness there is no verbal expression, for serenity constitutes purity."
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in that assembly named Dharmamati, who sat among the congregation and asked Mañjuśrī:
"If the Tathāgata were to speak of the matters of lust, anger, and delusion, would those not be the dharma of tranquility?"
"Is this gate of tranquility the dharma of stillness, serenity,
and purity? Mañjuśrī replied,
"What do you think, O virtuous one?"
"Where do lust, anger, and delusion reside?
From what do they arise?
He replied:
"From mindfulness, perceptions arise.
He asked again:
"From what do perceptions arise?"
He replied,
"It arises from habitual practice.
He asked again:
"From what does 'practice' arise?
He replied:
"It arises from 'mine' and 'not-mine'."
He asked again:
"From what do 'this is mine' and 'this is not mine' arise?
He replied:
"Existence arises from craving for the body.
He asked again:
"From what, in turn, does craving for the body arise?"
He replied,
"Because they dwell upon a self.
He asked again:
"From what does this 'self' arise?
He replied: "Mañjuśrī!..."
As for this "self," no place of abiding is seen; it has neither a location nor is it without a location. Why is this?
Because if one searches throughout the ten directions for the self, it cannot be found.
Mañjuśrī said: "It is so, son of good family!
If there is anyone who goes to the ten directions seeking a locus for the Dharma, it cannot be obtained, nor can it be seen."
"Why is that? Does that dharma have a gate?
He replied, "There is a gate of no-gate."
Mañjuśrī said: "For this reason, I say that all dharma-gates are entirely quiescent; everything that is taught is a gate of detachment, leading to stillness and purity."
When these words were spoken, eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, Mañjuśrī extensively expounded the Dharma for the assembled multitude, then rose from his seat and departed.
For this reason, Subhūti, you should understand this:
there are no disciples or bodhisattvas who can match his eloquence; how could we ever dare to engage in discourse on the Dharma with Mañjuśrī?
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti asked Śāriputra:
"Virtuous one, have you again seen Mañjuśrī? What extraordinary supernormal transformations did he display as he traveled to and fro, visiting various Buddha-fields?"
Śāriputra replied to Subhūti:

"I recall that in the past, while traveling through various lands with Mañjuśrī, there was a Buddha-field where fire broke out and consumed the world-system (*kṣetra*). Immediately, natural lotus flowers appeared, spreading everywhere in full abundance, upon which Mañjuśrī walked. In some places the fire blazed up, yet its flames were soft;

they were like fine, delicate garments, or excellent food of delicious flavor and fragrance, like sandalwood paste applied to the body, clothing, or bedding. From that Buddha-land, in the midst of space, natural palaces of Brahmā were spontaneously manifested, standing there in magnificent adornment."

At that time, the bodhisattvas entered into meditative absorption within them; in some Buddha-lands they manifested flourishing prosperity, inspiring all faith so that beings might attain the path of Buddhahood, practicing unobstructed compassion to universally save all sentient beings.
What is meant by practicing the compassion that is free from concealment on the path to Buddhahood?

Since all beings possess the fires of affliction—lust, anger, and ignorance—one who attains the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Path of Supreme Enlightenment severs these three stains and preaches the Dharma for the sake of the multitude. With a heart of compassionate pity, they enter meditative absorption with a concentrated mind; this is called practicing the compassion that is free from concealment on the path to Buddhahood.
"O Subhūti! Once, while dwelling alone, I thought to myself:
'I abide in this trichiliocosm, and by the power of my supernormal faculties, I am equal to Mañjuśrī.'"
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, knowing my thoughts, came and said to me:
"Venerable Śāriputra, you should cross over this world together with me by means of our supernormal powers."

"I exerted all my supernatural powers to cross the great fire, practicing with diligence day and night for seven days, until I and Mañjuśrī had passed beyond that buddha-field and reached the second trichiliocosm. That world-system was also ablaze with flames of vast extent, pervading the entire buddha-field;
Mañjuśrī then stayed there and said to me: 'O Śāriputra!'"
"By whose supernormal power shall we cross over to that world? I replied:
"We shall cross over to this buddha-field by the supernormal power of you, the virtuous Mañjuśrī."
Thereupon, in the mere instant that Mañjuśrī conceived this thought, he caused lotus flowers to cover that world and immediately departed, saying to me: "O Śāriputra!..."
"Whose supernatural power exceeds yours? I replied:

"To compare a wood-worm or a sparrow with the King of Birds, the Golden-Winged Phoenix, is as impossible as comparing these two to one another; the Golden-Winged King can lift countless bodies like mine in a single flight, such that they are no more than wood-worms or sparrows. The disparity in their supernatural powers is just like this."
Mañjuśrī said to me: "Why do you say, Venerable Śāriputra, that as you dwell alone in thought, you consider:
'The supernatural power of Mañjuśrī and my own supernatural power are equal'?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Judging by present practice, what constitutes wisdom? I replied:
"The disciple’s dwelling place has its limits yet remains unsevered and lacks comparison; when one sees for oneself that the limits of the dwelling place are severed, it then becomes equal.
Mañjuśrī praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Indeed, Śāriputra!

As you have said, in the past there were two rishis dwelling by the seashore. One was named Subhadharma and the other was named Dānaśraddhāstambha. Subhadharma had attained the five supernatural powers of a rishi with which he amused himself;
Dānaśraddhāstambha, through the recitation of divine mantras, could fly through the air."
At that time, the two rishis together set out from the seashore, intending to fly across the vast ocean to travel to the opposite shore.
The one named Śraddhādhimukta thought to himself:
"That excellent and wondrous Dharma and supernormal power are equal to ours."
Thereafter, they again flew together across the great ocean to the realm of the female ghosts (*piśācī*).

At that time, the rākṣasa played human music; when the seer Śraddhāla heard the sound of the music and saw the female ghosts, he was immediately terrified and fell from the void to the ground. He could no longer recognize his dwelling place by the seashore.
Then, during this period of the excellent and wondrous Dharma, [the Buddha] took pity on him, lifted him up with his right hand, and returned him to his former abode.
Mañjuśrī said to Śāriputra:
"At that time, the seer Subhavyūha was none other than myself;
the seer Śraddhādhimukta was you, Śāriputra."
"At that time, the Elder was truly not of their kind, yet he claimed to be equal to them;
now it is the same. Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"I further recall that once I traveled south with Mañjuśrī to visit various Buddha-fields. We passed through countless hundreds of thousands of Buddha-lands until we reached a world named Sarvavyūha-saṃpanna. There, the Buddha was named Guṇaratna-garbha Tathāgata. I went to that Buddha-field desiring to see the World-Honored One, prostrate myself, and pay him homage."
Mañjuśrī said to me: "O Śāriputra!
Do you not see all these Buddha-lands through which we have passed together?"
I replied, "I have seen it.
Mañjuśrī then questioned me:
"Śāriputra! How do you perceive these buddha-fields? I replied:
"Sometimes they see it filled with fire, sometimes incomplete, sometimes naturally like empty space, or standing by means of supernatural power.
He then asked me: "Venerable Śāriputra!..."
"How should one contemplate this Buddha-land? I replied:
"That which is full of fire should be contemplated as full of fire; that which is incomplete should be viewed as incomplete."

"Those who are like empty space should be viewed as being like empty space; those who stand by means of the supernormal powers (ṛddhipāda) should be gazed upon as standing by means of the supernormal powers.
Mañjuśrī said: "Just as is the sphere of Śāriputra, so too is that which he expounds."
I then asked Mañjuśrī, “Virtuous one,
how do you contemplate the buddha-fields?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Śāriputra! All Buddha-fields are lands of empty space. Why is this so?
All things are like illusions and transformations.
That which appears as a full conflagration is not truly complete; it is established by spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*) just as space is naturally so.
How can one speak of the causal conditions for its arising or the practice of its developmental stages?
“Space has no conditions and abides eternally by its own nature; likewise, though these various defilements of dust and affliction stain the mind, they do not establish impurity within it.
‘Śāriputra, it is as if all the Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to be engulfed in fire, yet space would not be burned; even so, Śāriputra!”’
If each individual commits as many fundamental unwholesome acts as there are sands in the Ganges, accumulating a multitude of calamities and evils, their minds will ultimately never establish purity.

If a man or woman can enter the pure dharma-realm, they will have no place of abiding nor any coverings, nor will they form conceptualizations; nothing can cause their minds to experience or abide anywhere. This is called the Dharma-gate of Non-abiding.

"By means of a single gate, one comprehends and governs all dharmas; one receives all dharmas without giving rise to various hindrances that obscure the intent of the Dharma, nor is there any distinction between good and evil.
Thus it is, O worthy Subhūti!
“I have personally witnessed with my own eyes the places where Mañjuśrī, through his supernormal powers and transformations, has preached the Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda said to Śāriputra:
“Indeed, O Noble One!”
I have also witnessed further transformations manifested by Mañjuśrī within the Jeta Grove.

I recall that in the past, when the Buddha was staying at the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery in Śrāvastī, he was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus and twelve thousand bodhisattvas.

At that time, heavy rain and dark, murky clouds persisted for seven days and seven nights. There were bhikṣus who had attained great supernormal powers and universally practiced the gate of single-minded liberation; though they did not receive food, they sustained themselves through samādhi and samāpatti. However, those who had not yet attained such concentration and meditative absorption had been deprived of offerings for five days and nights; their bodies were so emaciated and devoid of strength that they were unable to see the Buddha.
I thought to myself:
"These bhikṣus may not survive.
I then went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
"The assembly of bhikṣus has been unable to obtain food for five days; they are emaciated and exhausted from hunger, so weak that they cannot even support themselves.
The Buddha said to me, "Ānanda!..."
"Go and speak these matters to Mañjuśrī for the sake of the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, having received these instructions, I went to the chamber of Mañjuśrī.
At that time, Mañjuśrī was preaching the Dharma for Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings. I took this matter and informed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"The Buddha has sent me here to have you establish the practice of giving."
Mañjuśrī said to me: "Ānanda!
Arrange the seats; the time has come, so strike the ghaṇṭā."
I immediately accepted his instruction and, having gone out to arrange the seats, returned to his chamber. I wished to know whether Mañjuśrī had left the vihāra;

however, Mañjuśrī was still staying in the chamber, manifesting further transformations to preach the Dharma for Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings. He entered the samādhi called "Entering All Bodies" (*sarvakāyapraveśa*), a state of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), and then departed from the vihāra to enter the city of Śrāvastī for alms.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"Now Mañjuśrī is entering the city for alms while performing the lion's roar; I shall surely disrupt the merit established by Mañjuśrī."
Māra immediately manifested his power so that within the city of Śrāvastī, none among the elders or the multitude would welcome Mañjuśrī, nor would they provide him with alms.
Consequently, wherever Mañjuśrī went to the houses of the people, he saw all the gates closed with no one coming out to greet him.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, knowing the firm intent of Māra’s affliction, transformed himself into a brahmin and several elders, and immediately made this vow of sincere faith:
"If, by means of each and every hair of my body, all the merit and wisdom manifested therein were fully perfected;

and if even Māras filling as many worlds as the sands of the Ganges could not equal the virtue of a single hair on my body—if this is truly so and not false, then Māra’s transformations shall be extinguished, and he shall go in person to announce it throughout the streets, the neighborhoods, and the four crossroads, commanding the elders and brahmins to provide Mañjuśrī with the requisites for his alms-round, declaring: 'The merit of one who bestows gifts upon this man is the greatest; if one were to make offerings to all the attached beings in a trichiliocosm for a hundred thousand years, it would not equal the supreme and abundant merit of giving to Mañjuśrī.'"

"As soon as Mañjuśrī had made this vow, everything happened exactly as he had intended: all the gates were opened for him, and people went out of their own accord to welcome Mañjuśrī. Māra the Evil One entered every street and alleyway, proclaiming from house to house and at the four crossroads that among all commoners, elders, and brahmins, the merit is greatest for those who provide offerings to Mañjuśrī."

If one were to provide all manner of comforts to every person attached to worldly things throughout a trichiliocosm for a hundred thousand years, giving them whatever they desired, it would not equal the merit of properly offering alms to Mañjuśrī; the latter’s merit is far more profound.

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī transformed the food he had obtained so that it filled his alms-bowl; it was of various sweet flavors, each distinct and different, with every taste unique and not intermingled with the others. This transformation within the bowl surpassed the provisions for the thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus and twelve thousand bodhisattvas who had been invited, and it was just so.
At that time, after Mañjuśrī had completed his alms-round throughout the city, he emerged from the great city of Śrāvastī, and Māra followed closely behind him.
Then, Mañjuśrī stopped midway along the road, set down his alms-bowl upon the ground, and said to Māra Pāpīyān:
"You should lift up this bowl and walk ahead."
Thereupon, Pāpīyān attempted to lift the bowl from the ground but was unable to move it;
he said to Mañjuśrī, “I truly cannot lift or even shake this bowl.”
Mañjuśrī said to Pāpīyas, "You possess great power and infinite supernatural faculties; lift up this bowl with your great supernormal powers.
Thereupon, Pāpīyas exhausted all his spiritual might but was utterly unable to lift it; even through his transformations, he could not raise the bowl from the ground by as much as a hair's breadth.
At that time, Pāpīyān experienced something unprecedented and said to Mañjuśrī:
"There is a mountain named Īṣādhara; with a single thought, I am able to leap it into the air with my palm, yet I cannot lift this small bowl."
Mañjuśrī said to Māra Pāpīyān:
"The reason you are unable to lift and weigh this bowl is that you have always compared yourself to the great bodhisattvas; because you exert your strength upon this bowl, you are unable to lift it."
Mañjuśrī then rose from the ground, took up the bowl, and handed it to Māra, saying:
"Pāpīyān! You shall hold this bowl and proceed ahead."

At that time, Pāpīyas was deeply distressed and weary; he barely managed to lift the bowl. As Māra is the sovereign and most honored among the various devas, he was accompanied by twelve thousand devas and surrounded by his retinue as they held the bowl before him, prostrating at the feet of Mañjuśrī.
The devas said to Māra Pāpīyān,
"O Benevolent One, why do you hold an alms-bowl before Mañjuśrī, as if you were his attendant?
Māra Pāpīyān replied to the devas:
"One should not contend with those who are powerful.
He then asked Pāpīyas, "Virtuous One, you too possess great supernormal powers and infinite strength; for what reason are you unable [to prevail]?"
Thereupon, Māra Pāpīyas, receiving the holy command of Mañjuśrī, though he was a venerable deva, found himself unable to comply. Māra Pāpīyas replied to the devas, saying:

"The power of Māra consists of delusion, while the power of the Bodhisattva consists of wisdom; the power of Māra dwells in the acceptance of various views, while the power of the Bodhisattva understands the Great Emptiness;
the power of Māra is deceitful, while the power of the Bodhisattva is truthful."
The power of Māra consists of "mine" and "not mine," whereas the power of a Bodhisattva consists of great loving-kindness and great compassion;
the power of Māra consists of the gates of lust, anger, and delusion, whereas the power of a Bodhisattva consists of the three gates of liberation;

the power of Māra consists of the beginningless and endless coming and going of birth and death, whereas the power of a Bodhisattva consists of the patience regarding the non-arising, non-ceasing, and non-originating nature of phenomena.

When the celestial Māra Pāpīyān had spoken these words, five hundred devas among the assembly of gods conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, and three hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, Mañjuśrī and Māra Pāpīyān took their bowls and placed them upon the lecture hall.
The Venerable Ānanda did not notice this; when the time for the meal had arrived, he still did not see Mañjuśrī emerge from his room, and so he thought to himself:
"Could it be that Mañjuśrī intends to deceive the community of bhikṣus?"
"I should go at once and inform the World-Honored One, saying:
'The time has now arrived, yet Mañjuśrī does not emerge from his room.
Ānanda immediately went and informed the Buddha.
"I do not see Mañjuśrī emerging from his room.
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Have you observed what is happening above the lecture hall?"
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
I have already seen the bowl full of food upon the lecture hall.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Strike the *gandī* and assemble the community of bhikṣus.
I addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Yes, World-Honored One!
This great assembly of bhikṣus is so numerous; how could a single bowl of food suffice for them?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Cease now; proceed in silence.
Even if all the people throughout the trichiliocosm were to eat this food together for a hundred thousand years, it would never be exhausted."

Why is this? It is because Mañjuśrī’s holy intent and divine transformations cause this food in the bowl to be inexhaustible; it is established by the supernatural powers of Mañjuśrī’s perfected wisdom, manifesting the perfection of giving as a means of deliverance.

"Ānanda, having received these instructions, immediately struck the *gandi* to assemble the community of bhikṣus. From a single bowl of rice, there emerged various flavors; the delicacies were exceedingly beautiful, sweet, and rich beyond measure. It was as if many vessels each held distinct and diverse tastes, all of which were offered to the assembly of bhikṣus and the bodhisattvas, so that everyone was fully satisfied; yet the food in the bowl remained as it was, without being exhausted."
