Thereupon, the Māra Pāpīyān, wishing to disturb and obstruct the food offerings prepared by Mañjuśrī, manifested forty thousand bhikṣus.

They wore tattered, ragged, and filthy robes, carried broken alms bowls, and stood with their chests and backs exposed. Their faces were hideous, and they were lame, hunchbacked, and deformed; with hearts filled with anxiety, they sat among the assembly. They also took up alms bowls to receive various offerings, yet the food in those bowls was neither diminished nor exhausted.

The bhikṣus emanated by Pāpīyān ate to such an extreme that their bowls were not diminished at all; yet Mañjuśrī manifested his majestic spiritual transformations, causing the food in the bowls of those emanated bhikṣus to remain perpetually full. As they took morsels of food into their mouths, they became choked and unable to swallow; as they brought their hands to their mouths to eat, their hands stopped level with their mouths, and they all collapsed to the ground, unable to steady themselves.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī asked Māra Pāpīyān,
“For what reason do these bhikṣus not eat? Māra replied:
"Now these bhikṣus are about to die; could it be that you have given them food mixed with poison?
Mañjuśrī replied, "How could one who is himself free from poison go so far as to administer poison?"
Since his body is free from defilement and impurity, how could he use filth or poison to give to others!
Lust, anger, and ignorance constitute poison; for a bodhisattva who maintains the dharma-category of the code of discipline (*vinaya*), these various poisons do not exist.

What is called "poison" refers to the lack of wisdom in those who employ it—the attachment to craving and affection, the views of "this is mine" and "this is not mine," and the activities of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) driven by causes and conditions, merit and demerit. It involves creating objects of perception in an uneven manner; holding the view of a self, the various hindrances (nīvaraṇa), and dwelling in the grasping of the body and the fixation on thoughts. There are various kinds of sensations and sense-bases (āyatana), abiding within the three realms (tridhātu). There is grasping and receiving, there is abruptness and violence, there is going and coming. Hindered by the body and attached to the life-span, one remains close to and fixated upon perceptions, obscured by pure-mindedness and anger, failing to understand the root of the twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda).

They engage in disputes and cling to various views without severing their own preconceptions; they harbor thoughts and cognitions with arrogance; they differentiate between pure and impure perceptions regarding manifold phenomena; they claim that contemplating existence and non-existence, as well as all karmas and attachments, is "mine" and "not to be practiced," and thus they fear emptiness.

That is to say: there are two desires and two perceptions; one falls into the perception of existence within non-perception; where there is no vow, one gives rise to the perception of non-perception; where there is no attainment, one creates the perception of existence; regarding non-practice, one gives rise to various perceptions of practice; one gives rise to the two desires and creates the perception of deliverance; regarding the categories of the Bodhisattva-dharma, one forms the perception that they are not the Dharma; regarding the conduct of wrong views, one forms the perception of observing the True Dharma; and regarding evil associates, one forms the perception of them being virtuous friends.

They disrupt the Buddha’s conduct and slander the True Dharma; they are self-exalting and offer no protection to others. They regard contention, litigation, and verbal abuse as expressions of sincerity, and regard falsehood and deception as the ultimate truth. They regard the commission of various sexual desires as abiding in stability, and regard all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as peace and security. Regarding the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they give rise to views based on the notion of instruction, thereby destroying what is manifested in *nirvāṇa*.
Mañjuśrī said: “Pāpīyan!
Such practices of the Semblance Dharma (pratirūpa-dharma) are poison; they do not exist within the Buddha’s teaching.”

The teaching of ambrosia is the first of the Buddha’s teachings; the teaching of peace and security is the second; the teaching of heedfulness is the third; the teaching of freedom from resentment is the fourth; the teaching of non-attachment is the fifth; the teaching of the treasury of the True Dharma is the sixth; the teaching of non-contention is the seventh; the teaching of non-arising is the eighth; the teaching of non-clinging to self or other is the ninth; and the teaching of non-slander is the tenth of the Buddha’s teachings.

1. “The teaching that rescues through mindfulness and provides protection is the first Buddhist teaching; 2. the teaching of profound stillness and tranquility where nothing is produced is the second Buddhist teaching; 3. the teaching of purifying the pure through detachment where nothing is ignited is the third Buddhist teaching; 4. the teaching of bringing forth rectitude through the clarity of equanimity is the fourth Buddhist teaching; 5. the teaching of being free from anger and establishing oneself well is the fifth Buddhist teaching; 6. the teaching of honoring the most honorable by accumulating all roots of goodness is the sixth Buddhist teaching; 7. the teaching of liberation after having already been liberated is the seventh Buddhist teaching; 8. the teaching of transforming those of various heterodox paths is the eighth Buddhist teaching; 9. the teaching that for the wise there are no worldly desires whatsoever is the ninth Buddhist teaching; 10. the teaching that there is no beginning or end, nor death or birth, is the tenth Buddhist teaching.”

“1. The teaching on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the first of the Buddha’s teachings; 2. the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is the second; 3. the teaching on equanimity and abandonment (*samatā-prahāṇa*) is the third; 4. the teaching on the bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*), wherein no evil is produced, is the fourth; 5. the teaching on the twofold faculty of tranquility in body and mind is the fifth; 6. the teaching on the supreme power for the sake of the faithful masses is the sixth; 7. the teaching on the awakening of the mind (*bodhyaṅga*), wherein all afflictions (*kleśa*) neither appear nor do not appear, is the seventh; 8. the teaching on the path of universal realization through the understanding of the essence of awakening is the eighth; 9. the teaching on the silence of non-proliferation in all conduct is the tenth.”

"1. The teaching of serene non-contention is the first Buddhist teaching; 2. The teaching of coming to the definitive truth of liberation is the second Buddhist teaching; 3. The teaching of wisdom that is free from anger is the third Buddhist teaching; 4. The teaching that the meaning of the Dharma is inseparable from impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and sorrow is the fourth Buddhist teaching; 5. The teaching of having no self when faced with praise or abuse is the fifth Buddhist teaching; 6. The teaching of subduing all paths to attain tranquility is the sixth Buddhist teaching; 7. The teaching of reaching the mind of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*) and the perfection of crossing over (*pāramitā*) is the seventh Buddhist teaching; 8. The teaching of delivering others to the various shores by generating skillful means (*upāya*) is the eighth Buddhist teaching; 9. The teaching of protecting all living beings with compassion is the ninth Buddhist teaching; 10. The teaching of having no harmful intent and being filled with pity is the tenth Buddhist teaching."

1. "To teach that liberation from all possessions and donning the armor of virtue is the first teaching of the Buddha; 2. To teach that there is nothing to delight in, nothing to create, and nothing to speak of, yet being skillful [in means], is the second teaching of the Buddha; 3. To teach that having completed what was to be done, one gives rise to wisdom, is the third teaching of the Buddha; 4. To teach that without arrogance, one does not sever the mindfulness of the Three Jewels, is the fourth teaching of the Buddha; 5. To teach that by giving rise to the bodhicitta, one establishes all beings in purity, because of the non-arising of all realms of existence—this is the fifth teaching of the Buddha."
When these words were spoken, five hundred devaputras who had come from Māra Pāpīyān conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, and together they said:
"O World-Honored One!..."
"We, too, shall likewise revere the teachings of the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha smiled.
The Venerable Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"For what reason do you smile?
Since you have smiled, there must be a meaning behind it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Do you see these manifested bhikṣus?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
“I have seen them.”
The Buddha said:

"In the future, during the degenerate and evil age of the five turbidities, when the Dharma is about to perish, there will be such bhikṣus who do not know contentment and whose conduct is unwholesome; they cannot properly adjust their robes, and their natures are impetuous and lacking in serenity."

Why is this so? It is because, Ānanda, at that time those bhikṣus will lack reverence in eating and drinking, engage in various forms of slander, and seek to serve śramaṇas who have abandoned the precepts and transgressed prohibitions. They will drape their saṃghāṭī robes over their arms, show no respect toward the elder bhikṣus present before them, and their conduct in coming and going will be confused and disorderly. They will be frequently ill, and they will become śramaṇas merely to seek comfort and fame; they will only crave honor and respect, without keeping the Dharma in mind.
In that age, within my Dharma, there shall be such as these: people who lack insight and whose conduct is impure; all the devas shall be filled with sorrow, and Māra, the evil one, shall rejoice.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"For what reason is Māra joyful?
The Buddha said:
"These true men have themselves initiated the works of Māra; it is not that Māra Pāpīyān has found an opportunity to harass them.
Why is this? The wicked Māra does not seek opportunities against those who are indolent."
If there is a bhikṣu who practices with diligence as if his head were on fire, Pāpīyān will seek an opportunity against such a diligent person.
Therefore, Ānanda, you should exert yourself with vigor and not be indolent;

you should attain what has not yet been attained, accomplish what has not yet been accomplished, and obtain clear discernment to eliminate all uncertainty. You should subdue the hosts of Māra’s officials, promote the teaching of the Tathāgata, receive and uphold the True Dharma, and make offerings to the meaning of the sūtras—this is my instruction.
When these words were spoken, five thousand bhikṣus all relinquished their lives and entered parinirvāṇa, saying:
"We do not wish to witness the time when the Dharma is disordered and destroyed."
Sitting in mid-air, he emitted fire from within his body and performed his own cremation; thousands of devaputras together made offerings to his remains.

Two hundred bhikṣus were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, and the Dharma-eye arose within them; two hundred bhikṣus attained the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of outflows, never to arise again; thirty-two thousand devas attained the patience of compliance with the Dharma. Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and their retinues all joined their palms and approached the Buddha, saying: "O World-Honored One!"
May the Buddha dwell for a long time and provide extensive instruction, so that we may not witness the time when the Dharma is disordered, destroyed, and utterly extinguished.

Should there be those who hear this teaching of the sutra, they shall never be indolent nor burdened by defilements; they shall not cling to sensations, their mental activities shall have no fixed abode, and they shall give rise to no demonic deeds. They shall be free from the notion of self and have nothing to seek, just as the Venerable Śāriputra and the youth Mañjuśrī manifest supernatural transformations and preach the Dharma.
"Thus it was that I myself witnessed this at that time.
Then, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa said to Śāriputra, "I too have seen the supernatural transformations of Mañjuśrī; listen, O worthy one."

Not long after the Buddha had attained perfect enlightenment, when I was first shaving off my beard and hair, Mañjuśrī came to this world from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Ratnaśrī, desiring to see the World-Honored One and pay him homage by bowing his head to the ground.

At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, at the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery. When the three months of the summer retreat had concluded, Mañjuśrī did not appear before the Buddha; he was not seen among the assembly of monks, nor was he seen at the invitation assemblies, nor was he present during the recitation of the precepts.
Thereupon, when the three months of the summer retreat had concluded and the observance of the precepts was still fresh, Mañjuśrī appeared among the assembly; I then asked Mañjuśrī:
"O Benevolent One!..."
"Does the third month reside anywhere?
Or does it circulate through what is presented? Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Kāśyapa! I have been here in this city of Śrāvastī for three months among the palace ladies of King Prahlāda, and among the courtesans and children."
I thought to myself:
"For what reason do such people as these perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony for the Buddha together with my pure assembly of monks?
I immediately emerged from the lecture hall, struck the *gandī*, and intended to expel Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“My good man, do you see Mahākāśyapa striking the *gaṇḍī*?
Mañjuśrī replied to the Buddha:
"I have seen them, World-Honored One!
It was only because they wished to expel me.
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! You should manifest your own realm of supernatural powers and transformations so that Kāśyapa does not give rise to distracted thoughts toward you.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī entered a samādhi called “Manifesting All Buddhas and Their Lands,” and at that moment, he attained meditative absorption through this concentration.

As soon as Mañjuśrī had entered this samādhi, he immediately saw that in each of the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Mahākāśyapa who, being old in age, held a *gandī* in his hand and struck it, desiring to drive Mañjuśrī out.
The Buddha asked Kāśyapa,
"For what reason did you strike the *gandī*?
Kāśyapa replied to the Buddha:
"O World-Honored One!

Mañjuśrī has spent the entire three-month summer retreat remaining silent and unmanifested; he has gone into hiding and stayed in a secluded chamber. Therefore, we have struck the *gandī* bell, wishing to drive him out."
At that time, the Buddha emitted great rays of light from his entire body, illuminating the ten directions, and said to me:
"Kāśyapa! You should now observe the ten directions."

At that moment, he surveyed the countless and incalculable worlds of the ten directions; manifesting his own body as aged, he went before the Buddhas of the ten directions and struck the *gandi* drum, intending to drive Mañjuśrī away.
Furthermore, I beheld at the side of each of those Buddhas a Mañjuśrī residing there.
A Buddha spoke to me, saying:
"Mahākāśyapa!..."
Which Mañjuśrī do you wish to expel?
Do you wish to expel the Mañjuśrīs from the presence of the countless, immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions,
or do you wish to expel this Mañjuśrī?

I was immediately filled with shame and remorse; wishing to take the *gandī* and place it on the ground, I was unable to do so. I exerted all my supernatural powers, yet the *gandī* refused to fall and remained fixed in its position, unmoving.
Just as it is with this Jeta Grove, so it is with the Buddha-lands of the ten directions—there is no difference, for they are all truly and sovereignly thus.
“The World-Honored One said to me:
‘Only by taking refuge in Mañjuśrī can you be liberated.
I immediately prostrated from afar to Mañjuśrī, whereupon the wooden pin fell to the ground. I then stepped forward, bowed my head at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha:”
"I pray that the World-Honored One will forgive the transgressions and faults I have committed.
O God among Gods!

I have now witnessed what Mañjuśrī has manifested; even if I were to attempt to expound upon the wisdom of Mañjuśrī, it would be inexhaustible, and the conduct within the realm of the bodhisattvas is limitless. Because of my own lack of wisdom, I struck the *gandī* gong."
The Buddha said to me:

"As you have just seen, Mañjuśrī, who was by the side of the Buddhas in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, has now been absent from all those Buddha-lands for three months, teaching and instructing the multitudes."
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!

Within this city of Śrāvastī, Mañjuśrī has enlightened five hundred women and taught and harmonized the palace ladies, causing them to attain non-retrogression from the unsurpassed, true, and correct path. He has established five hundred boys and five hundred girls in non-retrogression so that they shall reach the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, and has caused countless people to attain the stage of a śrāvaka or be reborn in the heavens.”
I then asked the Buddha:
"What Dharma did Mañjuśrī preach that the people he delivered were as numerous as this?"
The Buddha said to me,
"Ask Mañjuśrī yourself what Dharma he has taught that was able to deliver so many people.
I then questioned Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī replied to me, saying: "O Kāśyapa! I preach the Dharma according to the fundamental dispositions of all people so that they may enter the discipline.

Furthermore, I instruct the multitude through play and amusement; or by practicing together with them; or by providing offerings while traveling for sightseeing; or by engaging with them through wealth; or by entering among the poor and the stingy to entice and establish them [in the path]; or by manifesting great pure conduct; or by manifesting transformations through supernatural powers; or by assuming the form of Śakra or Brahmā; or by assuming the form of the Four Heavenly Kings; or by assuming the form of a Wheel-Turning Sage King; or by manifesting the form of the World-Honored One; or by assuming a form of terror; or by being coarse and fierce; or by being gentle and soft; or by being false; or by being real; or by assuming the forms of various devas."
Why is this? Because the fundamental practices of people differ in many ways, and for their sake, various kinds of teachings are expounded so that they may enter the Way.
Indeed, Kāśyapa!
"By explaining five such dharmas, one attains entry into the law of ultimate truth.
I asked him: "Virtuous one, how many people have you delivered?"
He replied to me, saying:
"It is like the dharma-realm.
I asked again:
"How vast is the Dharma-realm?
He replied, "It is like the realm of empty space; all phenomena, the realm of empty space, and the human race are likewise so."
"These realms of sentient beings, the dharma-realm, and the realm of empty space are without duality, nor is there any dualistic construction.
I then asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
Although I see that there is a Buddha, will it not be of no benefit to me? Furthermore, he would be unable to provide instruction or deliver anyone from suffering.
Since the Buddha-dharma is empty and devoid of a person, who could there be to provide instruction and deliverance?
Mañjuśrī said: "Indeed, Kāśyapa!
It is like a person who has contracted a fever; that person utters various delirious words and ravings, and someone seeing this might say: "
"This person has contracted a spirit-induced illness.
Thereupon, a skilled physician arrived and administered medicinal broth to the patient; his ailment was immediately cured, and he no longer spoke deliriously or muttered incoherently.
"What do you think, Kāśyapa?
Could any spirits, ghosts, or devas possibly emerge from within that person's body?
He replied:
"No, it is because of drinking medicinal broth that his illness is cured.
Mañjuśrī said, "In this same way, Kāśyapa!"
"Does that physician bring about much benefit for them?
He replied, "Indeed he does."
Mañjuśrī said: "It is so, Kāśyapa!

Those people in the world who delight in deception suffer from the fever of affliction; they give rise to a mind of greedy attachment while lacking a self, yet they claim to have a notion of 'self' and thus fall into the cycle of birth and death."

Therefore, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world endowed with the practice of great compassion. To sever two matters and all conceptual activities, they employ skillful means to lead beings into the Dharma-gate. To eliminate the notion of self and the notion of others, and further to cut off deceit, they preach the Dharma for the sake of all people. To eliminate all conceptualizations, they cause beings no longer to delight in entering into notions of "self" and "other," so that they may attain the boundless and reach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
"What do you think, Kāśyapa?
Could there truly be a self, a person, a life-span, or one who enters parinirvāṇa?
He replied:
"No. Mañjuśrī said, "Indeed, Kāśyapa!"
One should understand this meaning: for what reason does a Buddha exist?

It is because his awakening constantly manifests the true principle; it is not by means of arising, nor is it by means of discipline, but rather because he desires to awaken those who are attached to and immersed in the dust and toil of the world.
Kāśyapa said: "It is most difficult.

Yet, when Bodhisattvas practice with such diligence, they don the armor of virtue to protect sentient beings and rescue all without abandoning them; they remain without attachment and without contention or turmoil, naturally pure and crossing over into the unconditioned, donning the armor of virtue for the sake of all living beings."
Mañjuśrī said: "Indeed, Kāśyapa!
For this reason, a bodhisattva dons the armor of great virtue."
Kāśyapa spoke again, saying:
"I pray that Mañjuśrī will explain the armor of merit of all bodhisattvas. Mañjuśrī replied:
"A Bodhisattva possesses thirty-two types of armor-like practices; donning this armor of virtue, the Bodhisattva comes and goes, moving about and circulating.
What are these thirty-two?"
Mañjuśrī said: “Indeed, Kāśyapa!
First, a bodhisattva dons the armor of virtue that enters immeasurable saṃsāra, protecting all actions from beginning to end as their natural characteristic;”
Second is the armor of virtue for delivering countless beings, which is free from the notion of a self;
third is the armor of virtue for making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, all of which take the form of the Dharma-body;
fourth is the armor of virtue regarding the various adversities, which is like the phenomenon of an echo responding to a call.
Fifth is the armor of virtue that protects all Buddhas, which is the mark of the equality of the dharma-realm;
sixth is the armor of virtue that subdues all Māras, which is the mark of purity amidst all worldly afflictions;

seventh is the armor of virtue that transforms all those of different paths through the True Dharma, which is the mark of realizing and entering the twelve links of dependent origination as being without fundamental basis, whether in terms of existence or non-existence.
Eighth is the armor of virtue consisting of giving all that one possesses without regret, with the vow to enter into the mutual practice and joy of all traces of activity;
ninth is the armor of virtue consisting of accumulating the merit of precepts and patience for the sake of all sentient beings, yet remaining without the mark of anything created;
tenth is the armor of virtue consisting of universally propagating what has been attained, yet remaining without the mark of anything reached.
Eleventh is the armor of the virtue of the power of great diligence, characterized by the emptiness and tranquility of body and mind;
twelfth is the armor of the virtue of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the single-minded *dharmakāya*, which removes all marks of attachment;

thirteenth is the armor of the virtue of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) free from all obstructions, characterized by the purification of all unwholesome states and the bonds of affection.
Fourteenth is the armor of the virtue of great skillful means (*mahopāyakauśalya*), which universally manifests all modes of conduct;
fifteenth is the armor of the virtue of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), characterized by the absence of any intent to harm;
sixteenth is the armor of the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), viewing the five destinies as being like dwelling in space.
Seventeenth is the armor of virtue of great joy, characterized by the absence of satiety;
eighteenth is the armor of virtue of great protection, characterized by remaining unmoved by suffering or pleasure;
nineteenth is the armor of virtue of fulfilling all vows, characterized by observing liberation as clearly as one's own palm, free from doubt.
Twentieth is the armor of virtue that does not contemplate any hindrances, wherein all darkness leaves no trace or sign;
twenty-first is the armor of virtue arising from the four great elements and the five aggregates, which manifests excellent and wondrous signs like illusory transformations;
twenty-second is the armor of virtue that regards the four kinds of nourishment as looking upon a venomous snake, with the dharma-realm as its mark of equality.
Twenty-third: The armor of virtue consisting of regarding all sense-bases (*āyatana*) as empty villages, such that no further signs of obstruction appear in any body;
twenty-fourth: The armor of virtue consisting of all that exists within the three realms, wherein no thought of existence arises;
twenty-fifth: The armor of virtue consisting of thoroughly and discerningly accepting all forms of existence, wherein no sign of arising occurs.
Twenty-sixth is the armor of the virtue of great valor, which is the mark of non-retrogression;
twenty-seventh is the armor of the virtue of great penetration, which is the mark of dispensing medicine according to the conduct of all beings;
twenty-eighth is the armor of the virtue of the great guide, which is the mark of manifesting the three paths.
Twenty-ninth is the armor of virtue that never severs the teachings of the Triple Gem, manifesting the wisdom-transformations of all Buddhas and universally demonstrating their meaningful signs;
thirtieth is the armor of virtue in which all dharmas are neither received nor produced, attaining the sign of the non-arising dharma-patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
thirty-first is the armor of virtue that abides in the stage of immovability, wherein one subdues all those who have transcended the disciples and pratyekabuddhas.

Thirty-second is the armor of merit that adorns the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); for the sake of practicing single-mindedly with impartial wisdom, one regards all phenomena as having the characteristic of authentic and correct awakening.
"O Kāśyapa! These are the thirty-two great armor-qualities of a bodhisattva.

If there should be one who believes in and accepts these thirty-two armor-qualities, even if the four great elements were to change, that bodhisattva could never be moved from the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
Kāśyapa asked again:
"Mañjuśrī! Among all the disciples, is there not even one who possesses this armor of virtue?"
Mañjuśrī said: "For this reason, O Kāśyapa!"
The disciples cannot don the great armor of virtue.
What do you think, Kāśyapa?
Is the same armor donned by one who is courageous and possesses great strength also donned by a base and unworthy son?
Kāśyapa replied, “No. Mañjuśrī said:
“O Kāśyapa! The armor of great virtue donned by a bodhisattva is such that no disciple or pratyekabuddha can don that armor of virtue.”
When these words regarding the armor of virtue of the bodhisattvas were spoken, thirty-two thousand devas and humans all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
Kāśyapa said to Śāriputra:
"Indeed, worthy one, such is the manifestation of the supernatural transformations and the preaching of the Dharma by the youth Mañjuśrī, as witnessed by my own eyes."
At that time, the venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to Śāriputra:
"Indeed, worthy one!
I too have seen the transformations manifested by Mañjuśrī."

I recall that in the past, when the Buddha was traveling through Vaiśālī, he was surrounded by a retinue of sixty thousand bhikṣus who made offerings to him. At that time, with my mind fixed in meditative absorption, I observed those of various paths and saw hundreds of thousands of people who were destined for liberation. I then went to the places where those of various paths gathered and preached the Dharma to them.

Having heard what I have taught, they do not accept or practice it; they do not take it to heart, but instead slander, mock, revile, and give way to anger. Having remained there for three months, I was unable to instruct or enlighten even a single person, and thus I grew weary and withdrew.

At that time, Mañjuśrī transformed himself into five hundred heterodox practitioners, acting as their own teacher, and together with five hundred followers, went to the place where Satyaka Nirgranthīputra was. He approached, prostrated at his feet, and stood to one side, saying: "I have heard that the Great Master’s fame and merit are celebrated far and wide;

for this reason, I have come from a great kingdom in another region to Vaiśālī. Now, the Great Master is my World-Honored One and shall be my Upādhyāya. I pray that you will instruct me, so that I may receive your commands upon the crown of my head and regard you as I do Gautama. I have never before heard the Great Śramaṇa preach such gentle and wondrous Dharma."
At that time, the naked ascetic Pūraṇa said:
"Excellent, excellent!
Venerable sir, before long you shall fully comprehend the practice of my Dharma and Discipline."
"Why is this? It is because of their utmost sincerity.
Thereupon, Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra addressed his own assembly:

"You all should be joyful and harmonious with these five hundred students, acting in unison and practicing together. You should mutually receive their transformation through the Dharma and study the meaning of the sutras together; whatever these five hundred people may say, you should receive it with careful attention and contemplate it well."

At that time, Mañjuśrī, together with five hundred bodhisattva-maṇavas and their peers, gathered and gradually manifested his conduct, his discerning merits, and his precepts; he then transcended his former state and universally revealed himself.

In the interim, he praised and spoke of the Triple Gem, and further extolled the virtuous conduct of the son of Śreṇika, Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra; having finished this discourse based on these causes and conditions, he fell silent and ceased speaking.
On another day, when the non-Buddhist practitioners gathered once more, Mañjuśrī said:

"According to what we and you, venerable sirs, have recited and expounded upon the meanings of your own scriptures, by this observation, the śramaṇa Gautama possesses the virtue of profound discernment."

Why is this? He was born into a great and noble family with a perfect lineage; his parents and descendants were pure, belonging to the royal line of a Wheel-Turning Sage-King, and he possessed the merit of a hundred blessings within a single mark.

I have heard that at the time of my initial birth, Śakra and Brahmā paid me homage, causing both heaven and earth to tremble; throughout the trichiliocosm, there was nothing to be grasped or taken up. Upon falling to the ground, I walked seven paces, raised my hand, and said:
"I am the most honored in all above heaven and below; I shall bring an end to birth, old age, sickness, and death for the sake of the multitudes."

The Dragon King spat forth water, and Śakra and Brahmā bathed him together. The devas and humans played stringed instruments, drums, and music; they emitted great radiance that brought rest to all the evil realms, causing all faculties to become complete, including those that were originally incomplete.
He caused all living beings to cast off worldly toil and anger, bringing them all to peace and security. A Brahmin fortune-teller had previously prophesied this auspicious sign:
"If he remains at home, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King; if he leaves the household life, he shall surely attain Buddhahood, becoming a Dharma King who turns the Wheel of Dharma."
Thereafter, having renounced his kingdom and abdicated his kingship, he sat beneath the Bodhi tree and subdued hundreds of thousands of millions of Māras and their retinues.

Having attained perfect enlightenment, he turned the Wheel of Dharma, which none could withstand; for the sake of śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, Brahmās, and the people of the world, he preached the sūtras and expounded their meaning—excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end.
That which is "good in the beginning" means that one's bodily conduct is good, one's speech is good, and one's mental intentions are good;
that which is "good in the middle" means that one’s intention is profoundly sincere, one is fully endowed with the precepts, and one transcends all worldly wisdom;
that which is "good in the end" means that one attains the gateways of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Furthermore, "good in the beginning" means faith in tranquility and freedom from negligence; "good in the middle" means the mind attains concentration and equanimity; and "good in the end" means that through right knowledge and vision, one realizes wisdom.

Furthermore, "good in the beginning" means attaining indestructible faith in the Buddha; "good in the middle" means attaining unconfused purity in the Dharma; and "good in the end" means attaining unfailing faith in the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, "good in the beginning" means not following the sounds of others; "good in the middle" means maintaining mental tranquility; and "good in the end" means the noble ones' impartial vision.

Furthermore, "good in the beginning" means cutting off suffering and eliminating its origin; "good in the middle" means practicing the Eightfold Path; and "good in the end" means bringing about the complete cessation of grasping and realizing its verification.
"This is what it means for these disciples to be good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.

Mañjuśrī said: "For the bodhisattvas, being 'good in the beginning' means to follow the intention of the Great Vehicle; being 'good in the middle' means not delighting in the intention of the Lesser Vehicle; and being 'good in the end' means to encourage and assist all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñā)."

Furthermore, "good in the beginning" refers to generating the compassion of an impartial mind toward all sentient beings; "good in the middle" refers to not wearying of great compassion for the sake of all people; and "good in the end" refers to the practice of protecting others with a joyful and impartial mind.

Furthermore, "good in the beginning" means to encompass those who violate the precepts and to cause those who are arrogant and lacking in practice to advance toward the Right Dharma; it causes those of a chaotic nature to attain impartial conduct, thereby eliminating perverse and evil wisdom.
"Good in the middle" refers to generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom.
"Good in the end" means that by upholding the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), one exhorts [others] toward omniscience (sarvajñatā).

Furthermore, being "good in the beginning" means practicing the four ways of attracting others to gather the multitude; being "good in the middle" means not sparing one's own body or life to protect and preserve the Dharma; and being "good in the end" means not falling into the various dark realms of extinction.

Furthermore, "good in the beginning" means holding the mind like the earth and practicing the bodhisattva path without attachment; "good in the middle" means being unshakable in wisdom and establishing oneself in non-retrogression; and "good in the end" means having no mental attachments and attaining the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood.
"This is what is meant by the Bodhisattvas being excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end.

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī preached the Dharma accordingly for the followers of other paths, causing five hundred people to give rise to the dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye, and eight thousand people to resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
At that time, the five hundred transformed beings prostrated themselves on the ground with their five limbs touching it and cried out with raised voices:
"Namo Buddha! We take refuge in the Awakened One!
The various non-Buddhist practitioners likewise imitated the transformed beings, prostrating themselves on the ground with their five limbs touching it and saying:
"Homage to the Buddha! We take refuge in the Awakened One.
Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately rained down *citta-puṣpa* flowers, saying:
"You all should hold these flowers and offer them to the World-Honored One."

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, together with the great assembly and surrounded by his retinue, went to the Kāliṅga Lecture Hall; having arrived at the place where the Buddha was, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

The various followers of external paths and their disciples offered these many flowers to the Perfectly Enlightened One; they circumambulated the Buddha three times and withdrew to stand to one side. Then, five hundred transformed beings, sustained by the virtue of Mañjuśrī, came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One!..."
We do not pay respect to seeing the Buddha, for the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body; we do not desire to hear the Dharma, for the Dharma is unattainable;
we likewise have no need for the merit of the Saṃgha, for the World-Honored One’s assembly of noble sages has no practice of congregating;
nor do we have need for the merit of the Buddha, for that Dharma-realm possesses no expansion of merit.
We do not require the Sublime Charioteer of the World-Bhagavān, for all dharmas are eternally quiescent and without a charioteer;
we do not require the meaning of the Tathāgata’s field, for those who are liberated have already transcended flowers, leaves, and fruit;
we do not wish to know the meaning of suffering, for our vow is non-dual.

We do not wish to sever habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), for all dharmas are truly without habitual tendencies; we do not wish to practice the Path, for that Path is already detached from both practice and non-practice;
we do not seek the realization of exhaustion, for all dharmas are eternally quiescent;
nor do we employ the cessation of thought, for all dharmas abide in non-abiding.
"We do not employ the merit of equanimity; that which is non-meritorious constitutes the impermanence of birth and death, thereby giving rise to all conditioned activities.
'We also do not employ the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*); we have no hesitant conduct nor any doubt, and there is no coming or going, nor the arising of birth.
We do not employ the sense-faculties (*indriya*), for to gain the sense-faculties is to lose their true meaning.'"
We do not employ effort; all existences and all phenomena are devoid of power and utterly feeble.
We also do not employ the intention of awakening (*bodhicitta*); all existences are eternally empty and there is nothing to be awakened to.
We also do not employ the Path; it is numberless and worldless, and there is no seeking of what is not beneficial.
We do not seek quiescence, nor do we seek detachment;
we do not possess the vision of wisdom that transcends the world;
nor do we seek to cognize meaning. Thus, there is always the meaning of liberation within the dharma-realm, which is without bondage.
We do not employ the meaning of "śramaṇa," for one who is a śāntivādin has transcended the six objects of obstruction;
we do not sever the outward form of a brahmin, yet thus being a brahmin, we do not sever slander;
we do not employ the term "bhikṣu," for that which is natural is indestructible.
We do not require the various *pāramitās*, for these six sense bases are to be extinguished;
we do not require contentment—why practice that which is insatiable?
"I have no desires, and I am likewise without any sense of satiety;
I receive nothing from the Dharma, and I likewise remain without speech regarding words."
There is no body, no mind, and no speech; yet we are not without abiding. Thus, the three realms are all equal.

We are not without that which is practiced as suchness (*tathatā*); there is no pleasure, nor is there unequal vision. We do not dwell in seclusion, for throughout the entire triple realm there is no practice of seclusion.
We, too, do not practice emptiness, nor is there anything practiced; this is suchness.
That which is undertaken and performed is also empty; we, too, do not beg for alms; this is suchness.
By eliminating all conceptualizations, we likewise have no fear of birth and death; this is suchness.
By seeing with precise and impartial insight, we likewise possess no lust, anger, or delusion, nor do we engage in slander; this is suchness.

Neither do we conceive thoughts, nor are we without thought; we do not sever the practice of worldly afflictions, yet we remain entirely unattached, responding in accordance with spontaneity (*tathatā*).
We possess no body and have no origin; such is our reality.
"This body is not a body; we do not observe it, nor is there anything seen in its departure;

it is suchness (*tathatā*). 'The Honored One has manifested his marks, yet we likewise do not remove any defilements; equality, impermanence, suffering, pleasure, purity, and self are naturally liberated. We likewise do not cross over the waters of the afflictions (*kleśa*); thus, we do not see this shore or the other shore. We likewise do not sever others, nor do we seek equal deliverance; it is suchness.'"

We speak of liberation as being without thought; we do not accept any state of non-arising or non-seeking. We desire that its primordial limit (pūrvakoṭi) be without arising or abiding, yet we do not eliminate hesitation, nor do we doubt the silent resolve. We likewise do not lack a right mind or harbor jealousy regarding our liberation through faith, nor do we wish to sever verbal expression; such is the reality.
Because we are liberated from the past and likewise free from conceptualization.
World-Honored One!
We do not even wish to attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), for all dharmas are quiescent and unconditioned.

When these words were spoken, two hundred bhikṣus attained the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of outflows without remainder. Two hundred other bhikṣus rose from their seats; having all attained the four dhyānas, they withdrew and departed, thinking that they had finally attained what they had not yet attained, and saying:
"The entire world is now thrown into disorder because of the teaching of this Dharma."

"We have previously heard that [the Dharma] is gentle and conforms to what is taught; yet the Dharma now being expounded does not accord with the Vinaya practice, nor is it the teaching of the World-Honored One."
Thereupon, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed Mañjuśrī: "O Mañjuśrī!
These two hundred bhikṣus have risen from their seats, withdrawn, and departed, saying these words:"
"Then, preaching this Dharma would cause disorder throughout all the worlds.
Mañjuśrī said, "O Pūrṇa!"
There is a reason for preaching this Dharma, which will cause confusion throughout all the worlds.
Why is this? O Pūrṇa!

The root of the world consists of the body, the five aggregates, the four great elements, and the six sense bases. Clinging to and fearing birth and death, one aspires for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); yet, not knowing that these are what is grasped within birth and death, one likewise fails to attain the compliant unconditioned.

Just as one who is sorrowful within the cycle of birth and death finds neither delight nor nirvana, so too, one who does not fear or tolerate [suffering] and is undisturbed regarding the four truths has no dwelling place; if there is any attachment, it constitutes delusion and confusion, and thus there is no dwelling even in the four truths of emptiness.
To be without contention or confusion regarding the Path, yet to become attached to the sūtras, and to desire to attain the Path—this constitutes duality.

Because there is duality, there is confusion. In this regard, for one who is equanimous, all phenomena are correct; if there is no duality, because of this non-duality, there is no confusion. To practice with the seeking of "mine" or "I" constitutes arrogance and haughtiness; once there is haughtiness, there is confusion.

If one does not have any attachment, does not perform any action, and neither constructs anything equal nor performs anything perverse; if one neither acts nor refrains from acting, and neither delights in liberation nor does not delight in liberation—this is non-distraction. Because there is no distraction, there is no duality.
And the World-Honored One said:
"I do not dispute with the world; it is the world that disputes with me. Why is this so?
The Tathāgata has severed the root of contention and disorder.
What is the root of contention and disorder?
It is this: "This is sincerity and faith; that is deception."
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"What is the speech of truth?
What is the speech of deception?"
"Since existence and non-existence are equal and without partiality or bias, what speech could there be to say that there is purity?

At that time, before the two hundred bhikṣus who had departed, Mañjuśrī manifested a great fire in mid-air that filled the entire buddha-field. As the bhikṣus sought to cross over it, they saw it entirely filled with fire and were unable to pass through the flames.

Desiring to fly through the void by means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), he saw an all-encompassing iron net in the sky and also saw great waters pervading the ten directions; so terrified that his hair stood on end, he saw from afar the path to Jeta’s Grove, strewn with blue lotuses, white lotuses, yellow lotuses, and red lotuses, and beheld a great assembly of people. He immediately turned back toward the Buddha’s location, desiring to hear and receive the Dharma. Entering Jeta’s Grove, he arrived at the Kālika Lecture Hall, approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Pūrṇa asked:
"Venerable ones, where have these bhikṣus gone?
From where have they come?"
The bhikṣus replied:
"O worthy one, we have attained arhatship; our outflows are exhausted, what was to be done has been accomplished, and we have attained single-mindedness, reaching the perfection of spiritual power."
Because we heard Mañjuśrī speak of the confusion of the Dharma, we rose from our seats and departed.

As we were traveling, we saw that the Buddha-land was entirely filled with fire; we were unable to cross over the great conflagration, and for this reason we have returned to ask the World-Honored One: what is meant by the stage of an Arhat who has exhausted all outflows?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Pūrṇa, saying:

"If one does not master the service of fire yet wishes to cross over fire, this cannot be accomplished; one will fall into the net of views. If one stands in conduct that is submerged in craving and desire yet wishes to cross over the great waters, this cannot be transcended."
Why is this so? Pūrṇa!
Since these bhikṣus have not yet escaped the fires of lust, anger, and delusion, how could they possibly cross over the great fire?
"Having fallen into the net of views, how could one cross the iron net?
Being submerged in the midst of the drowning of affection and craving, how could one cross the great waters?
The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"Those waters, fires, and iron nets come from nowhere and go nowhere; they are merely the manifestations and transformations produced by Mañjuśrī.
Thus it is, Pūrṇa!"

That lust, anger, and ignorance, as well as all views and attachments, come from nowhere and go nowhere; they all originate from the fundamental basis of conceptualization, discursive thought, and perverse conduct. These give rise to the appearances of "self" and "others," yet there is no self, no ego, and nothing to be grasped. By practicing solitary conduct and withdrawing the distracted mind, one gives rise to single-minded tranquility and accumulates meritorious deeds. With focused resolve, there is nothing to be attained, nothing to be conceptualized, and nothing to which one is attached; thus one enters into single-mindedness and gives rise to mindfulness of the sutras and the Dharma.
"What is the matter of the Dharma?
What is meant by the conditions of the Dharma?"

When one observes with careful scrutiny: having ignorance as a causal condition, volitional formations arise; having volitional formations as a causal condition, consciousness arises; having consciousness as a causal condition, name-and-form arises; having name-and-form as a causal condition, the six sense bases arise; having the six sense bases as a causal condition, contact arises; having contact as a causal condition, feeling arises; having feeling as a causal condition, craving arises; having craving as a causal condition, clinging arises; having clinging as a causal condition, becoming arises; having becoming as a causal condition, birth arises; and because there is birth as a causal condition, there are old age, sickness, death, lamentation, sorrow, and despair. This suffering, which is disagreeable, is called "birth. Thus, one comes to be joined with great suffering and affliction; this is called the nourishment of the body resulting from ignorance.

When ignorance is exhausted, volitional formations cease; when volitional formations are exhausted, consciousness ceases; when consciousness is exhausted, name-and-form ceases; when name-and-form is exhausted, the six sense bases cease; when the six sense bases are exhausted, contact ceases; when contact is exhausted, feeling ceases; when feeling is exhausted, craving ceases; when craving is exhausted, clinging ceases; when clinging is exhausted, existence ceases; when existence is exhausted, birth ceases; and with the exhaustion of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and all that is disagreeable are completely exhausted. Thus, this great mass of suffering is eliminated.

"To attain equality and reach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one attains tranquility (*śānti*) without conjunction. That which transcends phenomena does not perish; past ignorance (*avidyā*) does not perish, and future ignorance is not exhausted. Present ignorance functions through mindfulness; when there is no pure tranquility, ignorance is established. When the mindful wisdom is stilled, ignorance is not established. Once there is no establishment, that is eternal tranquility—this is called the exhaustion of ignorance."

By means of mindful contemplation of stillness and exhaustion, he observes the body composed of the four great elements as a body of delusion, like grass and trees. Even if it were to possess intention, mind, or consciousness, it would be formless and invisible; it has no sound and no speech. It is like a phantom, having neither interior nor exterior, nor anything in between, and nothing to be attained. For a bhikṣu who practices such tranquil mindfulness, there is no arising with respect to any phenomena; since there is no arising, that is the meaning of true emptiness.
When these words were spoken, those two hundred bhikṣus attained the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of outflows, such that they would not arise again.

At that time, Satyaka Nirgranthīputra, having lost his assembly of disciples, went together with five hundred followers to the Kālika Lecture Hall in the Jeta Grove. He approached the place where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings and conversation with the World-Honored One, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have heard it said many times that the śramaṇa Gautama uses illusory arts and sorcery to bewilder and turn away the disciples of others; today I have seen it for myself: Mañjuśrī has disrupted my assembly and increased the number of the śramaṇa Gautama’s disciples.
Thus it is, World-Honored One!"

Because they have received [the teachings] through wrong practice, they no longer come to me to receive my instructions, nor do they recite them; they do not employ my words, nor do they accept my commands with focused resolve.
At that time, there was a practitioner named Jayamati sitting among the assembly; he was a close friend of Satyaka Nirgrantha. On the road, he said to the Nirgrantha: "Stop!

Do not harbor impure thoughts toward the Buddha, nor harbor a distracted mind toward the Buddha, his disciples, and Mañjuśrī. Because of this, you will reap no benefit, and for a long night you shall find no peace, but will instead head toward the painful and evil paths."
"Niṅgañthas, listen! I shall now speak a parable.

Suppose there were a foolish person who, wishing to obtain clarified butter (sarpis), went about seeking it and took water, placed it in a jar, and shook that jar. In the end, he would only become exhausted and weary, yet he would not obtain the clarified butter.
Even so, Niṅgañthas!"
The practices of various heterodox outsiders are likewise; though they practice and study the Way, they cannot sever their deviant conduct.

It is like water in a large jar that cannot produce clarified butter (ghṛta); because they do not uphold the practice of the Tathāgata’s supreme and wondrous Dharma and Vinaya, they fall into hell after death.
For example, Nigaṇṭha!

Suppose there is a wise person, clever, intelligent, and discerning, who desires to obtain the cream of ghee (*sarpis*) and sets out to seek it. He takes milk and curd, places them in a jar, and shakes it; thus the cream of ghee arises, for it is by means of the milk and curd that the cream of ghee is produced.
It is just so, Nigaṇṭha!

If there are those within the Dharma of the Tathāgata—whether laypeople or those who have left the home life to study the Way—who with a sincere heart believe in the Buddha-Dharma and joyfully practice with diligence, they will swiftly attain the liberation of the noble ones, just as one obtains clarified butter from milk and curd.
For example, Nigaṇṭha!

Suppose a person borrows a hundred or a thousand earthen vessels from another's house and breaks them, but then repays the owner with precious vessels; would the owner then become angry or revile him?
He replied, “No. He asked:
"In this way, Nigaṇṭhas!

The disciples of various heterodox paths are like earthenware vessels that have been broken; they should now fashion new vessels of the Dharma-treasure in the presence of the Tathāgata, and must not harbor resentment or engage in verbal abuse."
For example, Nigaṇṭhas!

Suppose there is a leader for a group of people, yet he lacks skillful means; he leads the great multitude of merchants onto a wrong and evil path. If, however, there is a leader who possesses skillful means, he will lead all the merchants out of the wrong and evil path and set them upon the right path.
Thus it is, Nigaṇṭhas!

You masters, because you do not understand the meaning of the Path on the wrong track, lead countless people to fall into evil destinies. The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who understands the Path and its meaning, leads immeasurable people out of evil destinies and establishes them upon the right path.
"Then, the Nirgranthas departed, taking their assembly with them.

At that time, twelve thousand people left together with the son of the Nirgranthas; as for the rest, they all attained supernatural powers, and the World-Honored One shaved off their hair and beards, ordaining them as bhikṣus."
At that time, the Buddha said to Jayamata:
"Do you see these twelve thousand people who have departed together with Satyaka?
Jayamata replied:
"Yes, World-Honored One;
I have seen it.
The Buddha said:
"These twelve thousand people shall all, under Maitreya Tathāgata, shave their beards and hair to become śramaṇas, participating in the first great assembly. Why is this? Because..."
Because he has heard this profound Dharma,
Satyaka Nirgranthaputra shall become a disciple of the Tathāgata Maitreya, possessing the most supreme wisdom, just as my foremost disciple Śāriputra does.
"Why is this? Because one gives rise to arrogance and contempt toward the Buddha-dharma, and only thereafter abandons all views.
Then, the practitioner Jayamata addressed Mañjuśrī:
"In the future age of the five turbidities and evil world,
there will be many who are arrogant. Mañjuśrī replied,
"Yes, son of good family!"
In the future age of turbidity and evil, the multitudes—those children of inferior and lowly station—will delight in arrogance. Why is this?

Because they are unable to fully attain the four dhyānas, they fall due to their self-importance; during the time of the five turbidities and evil world, they will no longer make offerings to the assembly of bhikṣus, and these bhikṣus will find that their minds cannot achieve stability, let alone reach the fourth dhyāna.
Because there will be various defilements in future lives, and because in this world of the five turbidities many people delight in self-aggrandizement and arrogance.
In this regard, son of good family!
There are two things for which these sons of good family create arrogance; what are these two?
First, one becomes arrogant because of one's own insight and wisdom;
second, by using offerings of food and clothing to manifest one's own precepts, wisdom, and merit, one then falls into ruin.
"Those who are arrogant and slander the Dharma of the Tathāgata shall fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"By what means does one know that another person possesses a haughty mind?
He replied:
"A person of ordinary capacity has a distracted and unstable mind; this is not said of an Arhat."
"If one hears this teaching and feels fear, know that such a person is an arrogant, ordinary worldling.
One may see the Tathāgata, but an Arhat does not see him."
If one hears these words and feels fear, know that such a person is a conceited ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana*).
It is for the sake of the Benefactor of the Multitude (*sāstṛ*) that one should practice giving; it is not for the sake of a wise Arhat.
"If one hears this and becomes afraid, know that such a person is arrogant.
The Tathāgata praises ordinary persons, but does not extol arhats."
"If one hears these words and feels fear or dread, know that this is due to arrogance.
To not emerge from the various afflictions (*kleśa*) is to be without attachment; this is what is called being the most profound [benefactor] in the world.
If, however, one were to emerge from the afflictions, that would constitute attachment and would not be the one who bestows blessings upon the world."
If one were to practice in this regard, that would constitute arrogance.
To receive all dharmas merely as verbal expressions—this is called arrogance.
Not knowing anything, having nothing to sever, nothing to practice, and nothing to realize—this is what it means to enter into the ultimate truth.
He asked again:
"Mañjuśrī, what kind of speech is there for one who is arrogant because of their wisdom?"
He replied:
"I neither contend nor do I refrain from contending; I do not boast of my pride. It is like the lion, the king of beasts, whose roar strikes fear into all creatures."
In this way, son of good family,
a bhikṣu who does not delight in arrogance has no fear of any sounds. Why is that?

It is said that sound is like an echo; the response to that echo likewise possesses no mind, thought, or consciousness. It is because of the conjunction of causes and conditions that the sound and echo arise.
Thus it is, son of good family!

His mind and consciousness are thoroughly refined by wisdom; he does not discriminate among the sounds of various causes and conditions, for they are all like echoes arising from conditions, yet they do not originate anywhere. Those Buddha-sounds do not come from outside, nor do they differ from other sounds; there is no anxiety regarding the Buddha’s voice, nor does he perceive the multitude of sounds. Regarding the sounds of faults and anger, he feels no distress toward the clamor of the various worldly afflictions.

All sounds are without coming or going, nor have they beginning or end; this is the seal of having nothing to delight in. All speech is without high or low; this is the seal that establishes the seal of equality. Its characteristic is the seal of spontaneity. By means of this single seal, one enters the seal of the equal governance of the Dharma-realm: the seal of indestructibility, the seal of dwelling as it truly is in original non-abiding, the seal of the meaning of true emptiness, the seal of the equality of the three periods of time, the seal of neither arising nor ceasing, and the seal of spontaneous manifestation. With these seals one seals all dharmas; thus, there is no delight in what is delightful, nor is there any arrogance.
“Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu will have no doubt or hesitation, and he will not grasp at a self.
At that time, the practitioner Jayamata addressed the Buddha:
“O World-Honored One! O God among Gods!”

I previously heard from my friend, the heterodox practitioner Udayana, a discourse on the merits of this Mahāyāna; now, having likewise heard from Mañjuśrī the eloquence with which he has expounded it, I have resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

Therefore, I pray that the World-Honored One will preach the Dharma to me as is appropriate, so that I may be fully endowed with the factors of enlightenment, swiftly attain unsurpassed, right, and true supreme awakening, and instruct and deliver immeasurable, countless beings.
The Buddha said:
"Jayamata! I shall now explain for you the practice of a bodhisattva."
There are two dharmas by which one quickly attains wisdom and establishes the Mahāyāna.
What are these two?
First, diligence; [the second is...]
Second is non-negligence.
What is meant by diligence?
It means seeking all forms of Dharma-talent and giving them away without stinginess, not hoping for any recompense, but encouraging and assisting the aspiration for the Way.

First is so-called diligence: because it serves to sever all unwholesome dharmas, it brings all various virtuous and wholesome dharmas to fulfillment; one practices with an even mind and without negligence;
being pure in precepts, one does not aspire for any rebirths.
The second form of diligence refers to not being attached to body or mind, practicing patience without negligence, and protecting sentient beings with a heart free from malice.

The third form of diligence refers to accumulating all meritorious dharmas without negligence or a sense of satiety; it involves using all cultivated virtues and the noble methods of accumulating merit to encourage the aspiration for the Path.
The fourth diligence refers to being single-mindedly endowed with tirelessness and non-negligence in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), remaining without desire and non-regressive.

The fifth diligence refers to seeking extensively through broad learning, practicing non-negligence in giving, and constantly abiding in tranquility while honoring the wisdom of the noble ones (*ārya*).
The sixth diligence refers to practicing the conduct of the four debts of gratitude and instructing those who are heedless through skillful means and wisdom.
The seventh diligence refers to the actions of body and mind, wherein the body and mind are undisturbed and the mind is empty and quiescent.

The eightfold diligence means: for the sake of all beings, having a mind of universal loving-kindness toward all conditioned phenomena; being diligent in the meaning of the Dharma with a loving-kindness free from negligence; and being without attachment to any phenomena.

Ninth is diligence, which means to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment for the sake of others and all sentient beings; to observe all worlds without negligence, like a flame or a phantom, and never abandon the Way.

The ten types of diligence refer to performing deeds as if one’s head were on fire; entering into the ultimate truth without negligence, extinguishing [defilements] through the realization of wisdom, and practicing giving without arising [of attachment].

Eleventh, as for diligence: it means being fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks, accumulating roots of goodness, entering into non-negligence, and contemplating the Dharma-body as having nothing that arises.
The twelfth diligence is to adorn one's Buddha-land without negligence and to purify the realm of sentient beings.

The thirteenth diligence is to fully adorn and purify the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, to be liberated from all darkness and obscurity, and to delight in the Tathāgata’s and Bodhisattvas’ skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

All these are brought about through diligence; this is called skillful means and wisdom. When a bodhisattva receives this, they attain protection, do not regress, and establish themselves in the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

When these words were spoken, the Bodhisattva Jayamata attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Joyfully leaping up, he stayed suspended in the air at a height of forty-nine feet from the ground. The earth of this trichiliocosm shook in six ways, a great radiance pervaded the Buddha-field, celestial flowers rained down from the sky, and lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.

At that time, the Buddha smiled. It is the law of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, that when they smile, immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, and black—issue from their mouths. These lights pervade the infinite Buddha-fields, then return to circle the Buddha three times before suddenly vanishing into the crown of his head.
Thereupon, the venerable Ānanda adjusted his robes, rose from his seat, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and praised the Buddha in verse, asking:
“O Blessed One of wisdom-power and auspicious radiance, Guide whose light shines seven feet like a flower,
Possessing the thirty-two subtle marks And fully endowed with all the secondary characteristics.”
Like a lion amidst the assembly, his gait is majestic and his power supreme;
for what reason does the Buddha now smile?
We pray that the World-Honored One will explain it for us.
The Dharma he teaches is as swift as lightning; his voice is exquisite, like the lion’s roar.
Resounding with the resonance of precious jewels, its sound surpasses that of the Brahma heavens.
The Buddha’s speech pervades all people; its sound resonates throughout the three thousandfold world system.
It is always appropriate to every situation, and those who hear it find nothing that is not understood, for it is so gentle and supple.
You have spoken to the disciples concerning the pratyekabuddhas; yet their wisdom lacks clarity and excellence, and in the end it cannot equal universal wisdom (samantaprajñā).
It is likewise difficult for the assembly of bodhisattvas to reach it.
Who now shall obtain the power of such wisdom? We pray that the Guide will explain and deliver us.
Whether gods, nāgas, people of the world, or asuras, all have resolved their minds;
having been liberated from all sensations, their hearts hear that there is nothing to which they are attached.
Their immeasurable conduct is unimpeded, surpassing by countless billions those who are unequal to them.
Inconceivable and beyond calculation, you take equanimity as the measure for crossing over the world;
I now wish to ask about the true wisdom of emptiness—for what reason do you smile?
Colors of blue, red, yellow, and white, with various lights shining most brilliantly—
these wondrous radiances issue from his mouth, illuminating countless lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Pervading immeasurable hundreds of Buddha-fields, all elements such as the great [earth] are bodiless;
all are quiescent and nothing is seen, for the Buddha’s skillful benefit is free from fear.
When that radiance was about to emerge, none of his disciples could equal it;
they attained a brilliance never seen before as it shone forth, and the Buddha also spoke of the matters concerning the pratyekabuddhas.
Now I pray to understand the practice of the Mahāyāna, the supreme of all wisdom.
Its radiant flames enter through the crown of my head; that which has now reached me is free from defilement.
How excellent! It surpasses the gods and all that is venerated by worldly men.
I pray that you will explain the meaning with thorough discernment; not a single word of the Buddha’s is otherwise.
Having severed the doubts of the six assemblies, for what reason does the Perfectly Awakened One smile now?
Hearing the Buddha’s words, they were filled with joy and delight; countless people all leaped for joy.
The Buddha said to the venerable Ānanda:

“Do you see the youth Jayamati, who has leaped into the air to a height of four *zhang* and nine *chi*, remaining suspended in mid-air? Having attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), he stands with palms joined, prostrating himself before me as if standing upright, while hundreds of thousands of devas come together to make offerings.”
Ānanda replied,
“Indeed, I have seen it, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"This son of good family, Jayamata, has already served seventy-two billion Buddhas, cultivating goodness and accumulating merit. He has constantly acted as a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), serving all those Buddhas, World-Honored Ones. After the parinirvāṇa of each Buddha, he established pure brahmacarya under all seventy-two billion Buddhas and protected the True Dharma of each Buddha."
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!

This noble son Jayamati shall later serve and attend five times as many Tathāgatas as there are sands in the Ganges. He shall provide offerings and support their teachings while practicing pure conduct; he shall instruct and guide countless bodhisattvas. Thereafter, having accumulated the dharmas of awakening over incalculable kalpas, he will attain Buddhahood. His name shall be Tathāgata Jñānarāja (King of Wisdom), Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Teacher of Gods and Men, One Perfected in Wisdom and Conduct, Unsurpassed One, Charioteer of the Dharma, Honored One Above Heaven and Earth, Buddha, God among Gods. His world shall be named Priyadarśana (Joyful Sight), and the kalpa shall be called Ekaratnavyuha-viśuddha (Adorned with a Single Jewel and Pure).”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“That world, Abhirati, is like that which exists in the sixth heaven, the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Transformations; the dwellings and the offerings provided by the people of the Buddha-land of Abhirati are likewise so.”

For these people, no phenomena of the six sense-objects ever come before them; when all the people see one another, they are filled with joy and mutual delight, and upon seeing the Tathāgata King of Wisdom, they are all gladdened. For this reason, that world is named "Joyful Vision" (Sudarśana).

At that time, the Tathāgata performed the work of a Buddha for one kalpa as his instruction, and the lifespan of that Perfectly Awakened One was also one kalpa; therefore, that kalpa was named "Adorned with a Single Jewel."

That Blessed One has a retinue consisting solely of bodhisattvas; nine billion two hundred million bodhisattvas are all non-retrogressive, and these bodhisattvas have attained unimpeded wisdom and have given rise to the roots of merit of radiant light.
When that Tathāgata Prajñārāja was about to enter parinirvāṇa, there was a bodhisattva named Siṃhātikrāntagāmin who was to receive his prediction:
"After I have entered parinirvāṇa, this bodhisattva Siṃhātikrāntagāmin shall attain Buddhahood; he shall also be known as the Tathāgata Siṃhātikrāntagāmin, teaching within the world."

After that Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, his Dharma shall remain for ten minor kalpas. His relics shall be gathered together and enshrined in a single stūpa, measuring two thousand four hundred li in width and length, and three thousand two hundred li in height. This stūpa shall be constructed entirely of the seven precious jewels, and all people together shall make offerings to it.

Thereupon, the youth Jayamati descended from the void, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood before the World-Honored One to proclaim that the Dharma-realm is indestructible. He praised the Buddha in verse, saying:
“My lineage and the Dharma-realm, The person and the land are likewise equal;
This realm is the boundary of wisdom— By this, you grant me my prediction.”
The dharma-realm and the afflictions, And the element of space are likewise equal;
All phenomena are thus, And I have already attained this Dharma.
The realm of phenomena and the seeds of lust, And anger are also like this.
The realm of empty space is uniform; by this, he granted me the prediction.
The unconditioned land of birth and death is no different from the dharma-realm;
it is thus with the element of water, and likewise for fire and earth.
The aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, the eye-consciousness and all its constituents,
the mental faculty and the sphere of phenomena— the various factors and categories are all definitively established.
All these conditioned seeds, as well as the unconditioned realm, [are likewise determined].
Seeing no duality in phenomena, one is granted my prediction of enlightenment.
The World-Honored One has no five aggregates, no four great elements, nor any sense bases;
there is neither name nor form, nor is there anything internal or external.
The Buddha speaks by means of sound and bestows upon me this prediction;
herein all is utterly tranquil, and thus I receive this prediction with certainty.
The Buddha has no conceptual intention; it is in this manner that he grants me this prediction.
I am without consciousness; the Buddha has granted me this prediction.
This prediction is true and real; thus it is equal.
The dharma-realm is indestructible; such is the Tathāgata’s non-abiding.
"The Perfectly Awakened One among devas and humans, Upright in the True Dharma, as tranquil as space,
Perfectly endowed with skillful means and wisdom.
At that time, the clansman Jayamati, having praised the Buddha with this verse, circumambulated him three times and withdrew to sit to one side.
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Receive this sutra; recite, chant, and praise it, and explain it extensively for others.
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Having thus received it, what shall be the name of this sutra?
How should we practice it?
The Buddha said:

"This sutra is titled 'The Manifestations and Transformations of Mañjuśrī for Subduing All Māras, Converting Various Heterodox Teachers, and Receiving and Upholding the True Dharma: A Discourse Praising and Explaining the Meaning of the Sutra'; it is also titled 'The Treasure Store. You should uphold it."

When the Buddha had spoken thus, the youth Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattva Jayamati, the venerable Ānanda, and all the devas, asuras, and people of the world, having heard this sutra, rejoiced; they all came forward, prostrated themselves before the Buddha in salutation, and withdrew.
The Sutra of Mañjuśrī Manifesting the Treasure Store, Scroll II.
